## `scatterelements-add-existing-update` (use reduction=add so an existing runtime scalar replaces a constant update)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A `ScatterElements` writes a selected row, channel, or
bucket with a small positive constant whose exact value is irrelevant after a
later sign/threshold classifier.  The graph already computes a runtime scalar
that is strictly positive on every valid sample and has the right broadcast
shape or can be reused cheaply.

**Recipe.** Initialize the base tensor so the selected destination already has
the baseline value, then switch the scatter to `reduction="add"` and feed the
existing runtime scalar as the update.  The selected entry becomes
`base + scalar` instead of the old constant.  This is safe only when all
downstream tests depend on sign/order/positivity rather than the exact written
integer.

**Tasks.** task168 R9 changes the dynamic final ConvInteger weight edit from
an overwrite with constant `2` to `ScatterElements(..., reduction="add")` using
the existing low-byte foreground count `cnt8` as the update.  The selected
colour weight becomes `1 + count`, which is still strictly positive under the
final zero-point convention, while non-selected foreground channels remain
zero.  The standalone `upd2` initializer is deleted; local cost improves
`1271 -> 1270`, required splits pass, and the 98/100 promotion gate passes.

---

## `two-level-displacement-perfect-hash` (replace a large packed LUT with a small offset table plus compact code LUT)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A finite generator-valid signature set is sparse inside a
larger arithmetic key space, and a direct LUT is large enough that packing
bytes or storing high/low halves costs more than the lookup itself.

**Recipe.** Search a tiny first-level offset table `g[M]` and compact second
level size `K` so every valid prehash `h` maps collision-free by
`slot = (h % K + g[h % M]) % K`.  Store only the final byte code LUT when
`K < 256`; avoid high/low unpack chains unless the code domain truly needs
more than one byte.

**Why.** This keeps exact finite-domain behavior while replacing a large
mostly-empty table plus unpack nodes with one offset Gather, one Add/Mod, and
a small code Gather.

**Tasks.** task096 R7 maps 99 valid `(visible_count, max_variance)` clipped
ring signatures with a 29-byte offset table and a 63-byte code table.  It
deletes the older 314-slot packed uint16 LUT and byte unpack chain, improving
local cost `1675 -> 1630` with required splits plus 100 extras passing.
task096 R8 retunes the signature to a shared `[1, coord]` modular basis and a
64-slot displacement hash, then decodes the code with a small int8 classifier.
Power-of-two `K=64` keeps the modulo cheap and the classifier replaces the
remaining packed-code decode; local cost `1630 -> 1456`, required splits plus
100 extras pass.
task096 updated_v11 reuses the same displacement-hash structure with
`K=35/L=52` over `(visible_count + low(product variance),
product_variance % 35)`, after replacing the variance core by a 2x2
antisymmetric `J` synthesized through inactive coordinate scratch lanes.
The final QLinearConv weights are shifted so `w_zero_point` can reuse the
already-live hash modulus `52`, deleting a dedicated scalar and reducing
params `310 -> 287` at the same 956-byte memory.  Required splits and the
100-extra promotion gate pass.

---

## `onehot-lattice-mul-replaces-scatter` (use the detector lattice as the Scatter target)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A detector already produces a one-hot or at-most-one-hot
spatial lattice for each row/column candidate, and a later stage scatters a
per-candidate scalar back into exactly those same positions.

**Recipe.** Broadcast the per-candidate scalar over the detector lattice and
multiply:

```python
value_grid = Mul(valid_lattice, value_per_candidate)
```

This replaces `ScatterElements(base, recovered_index, value, axis=...)` when
the detector lattice is zero everywhere except the recovered location and the
value is already zero-safe for invalid candidates.

**Why.** `ScatterElements` usually needs an index tensor, a base tensor, and
often a separate invalid gate.  If the valid lattice already encodes the write
position, multiplication turns the write into a cheap broadcast gate and can
delete both scatter workspace and gating tensors.

**Tasks.** task397 R4 multiplies the exact 7x9 top-left lattice by the
per-column 2x2 distinct count.  This replaces the previous `Min` invalid gate
plus `ScatterElements` row write, reducing memory `1450 -> 1441` with params
unchanged at 69; required splits plus 100 extras pass.

## `sentinel-free-role-bank` (drop fake room/component ids when invalid coordinates can be all-zero)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output room/component solver carries a sentinel id
for invalid coordinates, tails, separators, or padding, but downstream
contractions only need positive evidence for real ids.

**Recipe.** Rebuild the role maps over real ids only.  Encode invalid
coordinates as all-zero role vectors instead of assigning them to a sentinel
class.  Move separator/border adjacency into a separate signed role plane only
if it is actually used by the final scorer.

**Why.** Sentinel ids often add a whole role column, index-feature table rows,
and final scorer coefficients that only cancel invalid support.  Zero role
vectors make invalid coordinates disappear from multilinear contractions for
free.

**Tasks.** task198 R5 replaces an 8-id room bank with a 7-id real-room bank
and separate adjacent-border role.  The final fused Einsum handles black
interiors, separator breaks, and separator preservation without the sentinel
or idx-feature table.  Local score improves `17.6329 -> 17.7551`; required
splits plus 100 extras pass.
task198 R6 is the next compression step: after invalid coordinates are already
all-zero, share the final channel decoder through a 4-D feature bank instead of
enumerating channel cases. The useful audit question is whether every invalid
or separator-only coordinate can vanish before the classifier; if so, the
channel tail often becomes a small multilinear feature table.
task198 updated_6 keeps the same sentinel-free direct-output architecture but
changes the room basis from a 6-D signed simplex with square-power margins to a
4-D cyclic Fourier basis with fifth-power separator factors.  Use this as a
search axis when a role-map renderer is parameter-bound rather than
memory-bound: higher polynomial powers can preserve separation after deleting
coordinate dimensions.
task198 updated_8 shows the next risky/slow compression axis: fit the two role
masks directly from squared 4-D cyclic coordinates, so the augmented constant
coordinate lane can be removed from the coordinate bank and role coefficients.
If a summed feature like `qsum = qmix.sum(axis=0)` only survives through one
lane, inline that sum inside the final `Einsum` by sharing the feature label
instead of storing a separate initializer.  This candidate drops params
`537 -> 441` at memory zero, but local promotion verification exceeds 60s, so
it must be Kaggle-probed as a slow variant.
task198 updated_9/10 moves the same direct-output solver to a 3-D cyclic
room/edge coordinate code and a joint wrong-minisize selector.  updated_10 then
removes the 4-entry `qsum` initializer entirely: represent the fixed batch axis
with ONNX `...` to free one Einsum label, and synthesize every `qsum` use by
row-summing `qmix` inside the declared output contraction.  Kaggle accepted the
slow probe, params `441 -> 352` at memory zero.

## `paired-side-count-tensor-selection` (select whole two-lane count factors instead of scalar lanes)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A solver computes paired side counts such as
`top/bottom`, `left/right`, `before/after`, then chooses an orientation or
case by selecting several scalar lanes and concatenating them back together.

**Recipe.** Keep the two side lanes packed in one tensor and make each case
bank contain the full two-lane factor.  Use one orientation `Where` to select
the whole A/B tensor instead of four scalar `Where`s plus `Concat`/transpose
staging.

**Why.** The lane pair is a semantic unit.  Selecting it whole can delete
small staging tensors and reduce transpose/concat overhead, especially in
direct-output polynomial or dot-power renderers where every lane feeds the
same final contraction.

**Tasks.** task093 R13 rewrites the horizon solver from `near+total` lanes to
direct paired `top/left` and `bottom/right` counts.  Whole two-lane A/B factor
tensors are selected by one orientation branch, deleting four scalar `Where`
lanes, two `Concat` staging tensors, two transposes, and a row-total `Gather`.
Local cost improves `818 -> 776`; required splits plus 100 extras pass.
task093 R14 keeps the paired tensor selection and applies the positive
QLinearMatMul threshold retune from
§`two-term-quantized-threshold-plane`, reducing local cost further to 773.
task093 R22 uses broadcast `Div` with static `[1, BASE]` lane divisors to
decode `[pack, pack//BASE]` for all rows/columns in place, instead of building
separate bottom/far tensors and concatenating them back into pairs.  This
deletes the two decoded staging tensors and their `Concat`s; local cost
improves `692 -> 667`, required splits plus 100 extras pass.

## `tfidfvectorizer-code-bit-lookup` (use TfIdfVectorizer as a tiny integer-code to bit-vector LUT)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A graph has recovered a small integer code and needs a few
static boolean/bit features from that code, but a full one-hot table plus
`Gather`/`OneHot`/`MatMul` costs too much or creates awkward shape staging.

**Recipe.** Cast the code to int32 shape `(1,1)` and feed it to several
`TfIdfVectorizer` nodes, one per output bit or sparse feature.  Each vectorizer
stores the accepted integer codes in `pool_int64s`, emits a scalar 0/weight
feature, and the features are summed/cast into the small code tensor consumed by
the downstream decoder.

**Why.** For tiny finite codebooks, `TfIdfVectorizer` can act as a static
membership LUT without carrying an explicit dense code-by-feature initializer.
It is useful when the next stage only needs a handful of bits, not a full class
one-hot.

**Tasks.** task392 team port uses six `TfIdfVectorizer` nodes to decode a
sampled-cell hash into code bits, then derives a small int8 stamp and feeds a
`ConvInteger` output decoder.  The port improves local cost `405 -> 348`; smoke
verification passes on train/test/arc-gen samples.
task274 confirms a smaller code-bit variant in a Kaggle-matched team batch:
a self-Einsum scalar hash is cast to int32, two `TfIdfVectorizer` nodes decode
2-valued and 4-valued bit contributions from `pool_int64s`, and their sum is
used as an int8 zero point for a `ConvInteger` decoder.  This improves
`mem/params 16/30 -> 19/19` despite slightly higher memory, because the dense
lookup table disappears.  Watch ONNX file size: vectorizer pools are operator
attributes, not counted params, but they still contribute to the 1.44 MiB
submission cap.
task088 updated_v10 shows a counted-memory micro-golf for this family: if a
packed token `top_code = row_stride * row + color` is already available, expand
the `TfIdfVectorizer` attribute pools to decode directly from `top_code` rather
than materializing `color = top_code % stride` and casting it.  The larger
ngram tables are scorer-free attributes; deleting the `Mod`/`Cast` staging
outputs reduces memory `166 -> 163` with params unchanged, while required
splits and 100/100 extras pass.
task367 shows that decoder width and renderer rank should be fitted jointly.
The old finite state used sixteen 2-lane TF-IDF outputs plus one scalar lane
with a rank-2 spatial renderer. Retuning to eight 3-lane vectorizers and a
rank-3 renderer reduces the decoded state from 33 floats to 24 and shortens
the sampled token document. The wider `P/S` factors add 36 params, but memory
falls `184 -> 128`; total cost drops `277 -> 257` and score improves
`19.3760 -> 19.4509`. All 29 known cases pass and HF confirms the exact
graph. Use `ngram_indexes` to assign several fitted features to one
vectorizer output, then search state-lane count against final renderer rank
instead of treating either width as fixed.

## `biased-log-bucket-tfidf-bigram` (replace exact bit-length decoding with a quantized log bucket and finite TfIdf dispatch)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A solver extracts an endpoint or run length from a packed
bitmask, but the exact bit-length decoder costs more than the downstream
finite case table.  The generator domain has bounded masks with comfortable
bucket margins, and a finite lookup can absorb the rare guard cases.

**Recipe.** Convert the packed mask/endpoint code to a float magnitude, apply
a biased logarithmic scale, then use `QuantizeLinear` to bucket the finite
generator-visible lengths.  Pack that bucket with the remaining discrete
geometry bits into a short token stream, and use a `TfIdfVectorizer` n-gram
lookup to emit the final stop/geometry selector.  Fold zero-length or
unreachable guards into the TfIdf table instead of materializing separate
exact-decoder branches.

**Why.** Exact bit-length extraction often needs `Log/Div/Cast` staging,
guards, and scalar shape adapters.  If the official generator only reaches a
small set of mask magnitudes, a biased quantized log bucket can replace that
chain with one small profiled tensor and move the finite corrections into
scorer-free vectorizer attributes.

**Tasks.** task066 updated_v17 replaces the exact left-endpoint bit-length
decoder from the v16 single-token TfIdf dispatch with a biased-log
`QuantizeLinear` bucket and a two-token TfIdf bigram.  It also probes the stop
condition directly from the black-channel bit and folds the `L=0` guard into
the lookup table.  Local cost improves `483 -> 459`, score
`18.8200 -> 18.8710`, with required splits passing and promotion extras
`98/100`.

**Limits.** Treat as probe-worthy unless the task is confirmed on the target
distribution.  The bucket boundaries are not algebraically exact; broad
fresh-generator tests may expose masks that fall across a quantization
boundary.  Keep the exact decoder or a safer previous version available until
the probe/portfolio result confirms the shortcut.

## `tfidfvectorizer-finite-signature-lookup` (use TfIdfVectorizer ngram attributes as a finite signature-to-parameter LUT)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A task's generator domain collapses to a small set of
discrete cases after a cheap integer signature, and the remaining solver only
needs a few scalar parameters or selector features for a direct renderer.

**Recipe.** Compute a stable integer signature with a low-rank moment or hash
Einsum, cast it to an integer token, concatenate/repeat the token stream with a
static terminator, and feed one or two `TfIdfVectorizer` nodes.  Store accepted
token n-grams in the vectorizer attributes so its output is the small parameter
vector consumed by the final renderer.

**Why.** The vectorizer is a static ONNX operator with compact counted
intermediate output.  For finite generator-domain lookups it can replace a
dense one-hot table, multiple `Gather`s, or fitted arithmetic that costs more
profiled memory.  File size still matters because the n-gram tables live in
operator attributes.

**Limits.** Treat as probe-worthy until individually Kaggle-confirmed for the
task.  The signature must be exact on the official domain; broader generated
extras can expose hash collisions, and large n-gram pools can exceed the ONNX
file-size budget.

**Tasks.** task119 team port hashes the rebound-V input, decodes line
parameters through `TfIdfVectorizer`, and renders with one final Einsum.  The
2026-06-24 confirmed team version trims this further to memory/params
`44/105`, score `19.9961`, by using one repeated token stream and the
vectorizer's n-gram attribute table instead of an explicit dense
signature-to-parameter table.  Earlier local variants were
`66/99 -> 52/103`, so recheck both counted cost and ONNX file size after every
pool retune.
task310 uses the safer one-token class-LUT form inside a larger renderer:
an `ArgMax` over a compact count signature feeds a single `TfIdfVectorizer`
whose output is the selected colour one-hot vector.  This replaces a
Gather/OneHot adapter before row/column rank decoding and was confirmed at
memory/params `156/209`, score `19.1001`.
task148 updated_v1 uses a row-state hash as the token instead of a class id:
an output `Einsum` hashes red row intervals plus the cyan row subset, repeats
the hash seven times with a static terminator, then seven `TfIdfVectorizer`
nodes decode the transition bit and odd destination-row coordinate roots needed
by the unchanged portal renderer.  The vectorizer pools are large, so file size
is near the limit, but counted cost improves `127/117 -> 96/125` and required
splits plus 100/100 extras pass locally.

task148 updated_v4 compresses the same finite row-state decoder further by
using only four repeated hash tokens plus a zero terminator.  The hash is
rebuilt from renderer constants already in the final `Einsum` (`U/P/CB/Ffac/PA`)
and scaled by three fully contracted `PA` operands, which keeps the serialized
TfIdf attribute tables under the model-size limit without adding counted
params.  Memory/params improve `96/125 -> 84/113` (cost `221 -> 197`) with
required splits and 100/100 extras passing.

The zero terminator costs one int32 initializer, but deleting the longer
hash-token stream saves more profiled bytes; a global zero-token row offset and

`197 -> 189` from the confirmed v4 baseline, and required splits plus 100/100

task187 updated_v56 uses `TfIdfVectorizer` as a compact static marker expander:
cast the row/column `TopK` indices to int32, concatenate them with a synthetic
first-row marker, then a single vectorizer emits a 3-row marker tensor whose
`CumSum(axis=1)` is the old `[ones,row_code,col_code]` `pair3` basis.  This
deletes the `ones_f30` initializer, separate row/column `MaxUnpool + CumSum`

`1455 -> 1384`, local score `17.7172 -> 17.7673`, required splits and 100/100

task284 updated_v8 uses a finite-signature vectorizer as a compact bigram
channel router for the scratch/diff-scale synthesis path.  The signature emits

task284 updated_v9 retunes the same finite-signature endpoint-colour solver by

## `tfidfvectorizer-roi-attribute-lut` (use TfIdfVectorizer attributes to emit RoiAlign box coordinates)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task can be reduced to a finite signature, and the
remaining operation is a crop/resample that can be expressed by one
`RoiAlign` box.  A dense signature-to-ROI initializer or `Gather` table would
cost params, while the ROI table is large but still fits under the ONNX file
size cap.

**Recipe.** Compute a small integer signature, cast it to int32, repeat it
into a short token stream, and feed one `TfIdfVectorizer` whose n-gram
attributes emit a `[1, 4]` fp32 `rois` tensor.  Use a one-element `batch`
initializer for the `RoiAlign` batch indices, then let `RoiAlign` produce the
graph output directly.

**Why.** `TfIdfVectorizer` stores the finite lookup in operator attributes, not
counted initializers.  For ROI-driven geometry this can replace a counted
four-float ROI initializer table plus decode logic with one tiny counted
intermediate and one scalar initializer.  The final `RoiAlign` output is the
graph output, so the scorer only charges the signature/ROI intermediates.

**Limits.** Attribute tables still count toward the 1.44 MiB ONNX size limit.
This is only safe when the signature is exact on the official domain; broader
extra generators can create unseen signatures or hash collisions.  Treat new
uses as probe-worthy until Kaggle-confirmed.

**Tasks.** task021 uses a six-copy signature token stream with one
`TfIdfVectorizer` to emit a `[1,4]` ROI box, then one `RoiAlign` resamples the
input directly to output.  The Kaggle-confirmed team promotion improves
`memory/params 48/2 -> 48/1`, score `21.0880 -> 21.1082`, with the large
signature table living in attributes rather than counted params.
The 2026-07-05 HF leaderboard version retunes the same TfIdf/RoiAlign
signature so the ROI path is `memory/params 44/2` (`cost 46`, score
`21.1714`); the attribute table remains uncounted, but the exact-signature
caveat still applies.
The 2026-07-06 HF leaderboard version removes another counted ROI staging lane,
reaching `memory/params 36/2` (`cost 38`, score `21.3624`) while keeping the
same one-vectorizer-to-RoiAlign structure.
task355 updated_v23 uses the same attribute-LUT idea with a self-`Einsum`
hash and sentinel-separated token stream.  `TfIdfVectorizer` emits the ROI box
for the quadrant winner, and one `RoiAlign` renders the selected color over
the output.  HF accepted the graph at `memory/params 40/2` (`cost 42`, score
`21.2623`), improving the previous local production cost `102 -> 42`.
task355 updated_v24 shrinks the same RoiAlign lookup by changing the token
stream to `[hash, sentinel, hash]` and enabling skip-grams (`max_skip_count=1`).
The sentinel unigram supplies a fixed ROI offset and the hash-specific
unigrams/bigrams/trigrams supply only the remaining coordinate units.  This
keeps the large table in attributes but deletes four counted ROI bytes:
`memory/params 40/2 -> 36/2` (`cost 42 -> 38`), with HF scoring the graph at
`21.3624`.

## `maxunpool-as-sparse-scatter` (use MaxUnpool as a static-shape sparse scatter from values and flat indices)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A solution has a short vector of values and exact flattened
destination indices for those values, and the target canvas shape is static.

**Recipe.** Cast values to a compact numeric type, cast flat indices to int64,
and call `MaxUnpool(values, indices, output_shape)`.  Use the static
`output_shape` initializer to place the sparse vector into the full output
canvas in one op.

**Why.** `MaxUnpool` can replace a zero canvas plus `ScatterElements` or
`ScatterND` when the update positions are already known as flattened indices.
It keeps the destination shape static and can avoid carrying a large zero base
or rank-expanded scatter index tensor.

**Tasks.** task178 team port compacts five labels, computes flat offsets as
`label * 900 + location`, and uses `MaxUnpool` to scatter them into the
`(1,10,30,30)` output.  The port improves local cost `380 -> 368`; smoke
verification passes on train/test/arc-gen samples.
task178 updated_v41 continues the same sparse-label scatter chain and deletes
one more generator-tail RLE scalar by routing `code12` directly into the
remaining tail case.  Memory drops `218 -> 217` at unchanged params `54`;
required splits pass and promotion extras are `99/100`, which is above the
portfolio-safe threshold.
The 2026-06-28 team batch confirms a further retune of the same MaxUnpool
scatter chain, reducing cost `266 -> 256` and score
`19.4165 -> 19.4548`.  task115 updated_v1 uses `TopK` values as the sparse
payloads and computes flattened destinations `colour * 900 + slot` or
`colour * 900 + 30 * slot` for row/column one-line outputs, replacing a
small-work-canvas `QLinearConv` tail with `MaxUnpool`.  updated_v6 folds the
row/column offset tables into one `slot * stride` expression and retunes the
geometric priority scale/floor for stable far-coordinate ordering.  Final cost
drops `217 -> 203` with required splits plus 100/100 extras passing.
task178 updated_v4 shows that the sparse-label tail is worth pruning after
every retune: once `MaxUnpool` only needs the final compact label vector and
flat indices, late bounded-RLE branch aliases can be folded away even if they
look like useful intermediates.  Deleting five one-byte branch tensors reduces
cost `256 -> 251`, with required splits and 98/100 promotion extras passing.
task115 updated_v14 removes the stored `900` multiplier and separate base
tensor in the flat-index tail.  It casts the TopK colour ids and slot vector
to fp16, builds `zslot = 0 if row_mode else slot`, then computes
`slot + 29*zslot + 900*colour_id` by passing `idx_h` 900 times and `zslot`
29 times to one variadic `Sum`; the scorer charges the repeated inputs only
for the original small tensors.  Cost improves `203 -> 190` with required
splits plus 100/100 extras passing.
task346 updated_v3 uses the degenerate case where there is exactly one output
cell: a scalar weighted-colour decoder produces the selected colour, `Mul(900)`
turns it into the flattened channel offset, and `MaxUnpool` writes the scalar
positive logit at `(colour,0,0)`.  This replaces a full-canvas direct `Einsum`

task346 updated_v6 keeps the same sparse one-cell scatter but changes the flat

`QuantizeLinear(UINT8) -> DequantizeLinear(fp16 scale=900) -> Cast(INT64)`.
The legal channel offsets are exact in fp16, so this deletes one counted

## `row-sum-tied-interval-separator` (derive the paired upper test from an existing embedding row sum)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A direct-output `Einsum` uses paired lower/upper linear
separators over the same finite-domain scalar features, and one side is a
simple affine retune of the other.  The graph already carries a channel or
feature embedding whose row sums can supply the needed multipliers.

**Recipe.** Store only the lower separator matrix.  Pass the same matrix
through the final contraction twice: once directly for the lower logit and once
with an extra shared embedding axis whose row sum transforms the stored
coefficients into the upper separator.  Retune the embedding row sums so they
still provide the output-channel signs while also producing the paired
separator coefficients.

**Why.** This deletes the separate upper-separator initializer while preserving
two-sided finite-domain gating.  It is most useful for memory-free
direct-output `Einsum` graphs where parameters dominate the score and the
paired predicates are fitted to public/generator coverage.  Because the
separator is a fitted shortcut, probe if extras or hidden coverage are not
fully convincing.

**Tasks.** task070 v7 stores one 2x3 separator `D` and derives the upper
hidden-column test via `sum_K G[v,K] = [1, 0.25, -1]`, while the same `G` row
sums also provide output channel signs.  Kaggle accepted the probe and local
promotion passed required splits plus 100/100 extras, reducing params
`56 -> 46` at memory zero.

## `fp32-underflow-tied-sign-vector` (tie a zero-suppressed output sign to a nonzero source sign)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-free direct-output `Einsum` carries two nearly
identical channel sign vectors: one where a special colour must remain
negative as an input/source factor, and another where that same colour must be
zero or non-positive as an output-channel factor.

**Recipe.** Store one fp32 vector `r`.  Use `r[d]` once for the source/local
polarity and repeat the output-channel label enough times to form `r[c]**k`.
Set the special colour to a tiny negative fp32 value such as `-1e-16`.  It
stays strictly negative when used once, but underflows to signed zero after a
cubic product in ONNX Runtime fp32 `Einsum`; the verifier's `output > 0`
threshold then suppresses that channel without a second initializer.

**Why.** This can delete a whole channel-sign initializer in direct-output
graphs where params dominate and the output threshold only cares about
positive logits.  Keep it to small fp32 products tested under the target ORT
version; avoid it when downstream arithmetic distinguishes signed zero or
depends on exact nonzero magnitudes.

**Tasks.** task312 updated_3 ties `cell_sign` and `channel_sign` into one
10-entry vector: gray is `-1e-16`, so gray cells still route through the row
marker as a negative source factor, while `r[gray]**3` underflows to zero for
the gray output channel.  Local promotion passed required splits plus 100/100
extras, reducing params `20 -> 10` at memory zero.
task141 updated uses the same one-vector idea without an output power:
`r[0] = -1e-30` is negligible when summing foreground seed moments, but it is
still a strictly negative black-channel output sign.  This deletes the separate
foreground selector from the direct diagonal-X Einsum, reducing params
`88 -> 78` at memory zero with 100/100 extras.
task197 updated_v1 extends the trick by using one vector for three roles:
`r[0] = 1e-10`, `r[1..9] = -1`; six repeated `r[d]` operands synthesize the
reference-row nonblack selector because black underflows through `r[d]**6` to
zero while nonblack stays `+1`.  The same `r[c]`/`r[o]` factors provide row and
output polarity.  This deletes the separate nonblack/sign vector, reducing
params `20 -> 10` at memory zero with required splits and 100/100 extras
passing.

## `fp32-underflow-branch-channel-code` (use one short channel code where a special row is positive once but zero after squaring)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct-output `Einsum` needs a small
channel-role gate such as "black preserves black, nonblack routes to one
foreground branch, but one special foreground colour must be suppressed as an
output channel".  The graph can repeat the channel code on the output-channel
axis more times than on the source/input axis.

**Recipe.** Store a short code `F[color, branch]`.  Give the special colour a
tiny positive branch value `eps`, for example `1e-24`.  Use `F[source,branch]`
once where the source colour must remain live, but use `F[output,branch]**2`
or a higher power in the output gate.  Under ORT fp32, `eps` remains strictly
positive when used once and underflows to `+0.0` when squared, so
`output > 0` accepts the source contribution while suppressing that output
channel.

**Why.** This can replace a separate quadratic channel-gate tensor with one
short branch code, keeping the whole renderer as the graph output and reducing
counted params.  It is safer than threshold underflow when the only
underflowed value is an intentionally inactive output channel and the source
path still has a large margin.

**Limits.** Confirm under the target ORT version and keep a normal-margin
backup if the graph also relies on cancellation between large terms.  Do not
use it when downstream ops distinguish tiny positives from zero instead of the
verifier's final `> 0` threshold.

**Tasks.** task354 updated_v25 replaces the 28-param `T/H` quadratic channel
gate with a 20-param `F[10,2]` code: black uses branch 0, nonblack uses branch
1, and gray sets `F[5,1]=1e-24`, so gray remains positive as a source row
factor but `F[5,1]**2` underflows in the output-channel gate.  Cost drops
`148 -> 140` at memory zero with required splits and 100/100 extras passing.

---

## `z3-finite-domain-sign-polynomial-search` (synthesize small sign polynomials before wiring a direct-output graph)
**Status:** operational

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct-output graph would be driven by a
small finite-domain sign predicate such as "middle vs non-middle", "same color
vs black", or "one generator-bounded branch vs another", and the main unknown
is the coefficient pattern rather than the task semantics.

**Recipe.** Write a bounded Z3 search over the exact generator domain and the
features that can realistically be represented in ONNX, for example
`A=(j-k)^2`, `K=k^2`, `B=((2*c+1)-N)^2`.  Constrain positives to `>= margin`
and negatives to `<= -margin`, then minimize coefficient absolute values
before maximizing margin.  Keep the script in `src/search/` so UNSAT results
and found constants are reproducible.

**Why.** This avoids manual coefficient guessing for direct `Einsum`
classifiers and quickly rejects feature families that cannot separate the
finite generator states.  It is especially useful before attempting expensive
single-Einsum rewrites where a failed sign family can waste substantial ONNX
debugging time.

**Limits.** A satisfiable polynomial is not automatically a lower-cost ONNX
graph.  The feature family must map to existing tables/factors without adding
more params or memory than it removes.  Treat this as a search/proof tool, then
run the normal promotion or variant workflow.

**Tasks.** task329 search `src/search/task329_z3_middle_column_polynomial.py`
proves a compact semantic separator for the odd-square middle-column rule:
`score = 1 - 2A + A*B - 63*K*B`, where `A=(j-k)^2`, `K=k^2`, and
`B=((2*c+1)-N)^2`.  The family is valid on the full finite generator domain,
but the current ONNX mapping still needs the same shared feature tables/core as
the 88-param production graph, so it is documented for future retunes rather
than promoted.

---

## `cp-factorized-cubic-core-einsum` (replace a dense 2x2x2xV cubic map with low-rank linear factors inside the final Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct-output `Einsum` already synthesizes a
second finite-domain classifier row/vector from a compact code by applying a
dense cubic core such as `C[a,b,c,v]`.  If the finite set of code points is
small, fit a CP/Waring-style factorization offline:

```python
R2[o,v] = sum_q V[v,q] * (sum_a R1[o,a] * U[a,q])**3
```

Then expand the cube by repeating the `R1,U` operands three times in the final
`Einsum`.  This deletes the dense cubic-core initializer at the cost of two
small factor matrices, while keeping graph memory at zero because the
factorization is evaluated only in the graph-output contraction.

**Limits.**
- The factorization only has to preserve signs/margins on the generator-valid
  finite domain, but it should be smoke-tested under the target ORT because
  contraction order and fp32 cancellation can change tiny margins.
- Check the `Einsum` label budget before increasing rank.  Rank 3 was still
  small enough for task010; higher rank may erase the params win or become
  slow.

**Tasks.** task010 updated_v12 replaces dense `C3[2,2,2,2]` (16 params) with
`U[2,3] + V[2,3]` (12 params), reducing total params `56 -> 52`, memory `0`,
and passing promotion extras `100/100`.  task010 updated_v15_fast reuses the
existing shared `E[10,2]` table as the cubic basis and stores only `W[10]`,
reducing params `52 -> 50`; placing the output-sized local-role term last in
the `Einsum` operand list also cuts ORT required-split runtime from tens of
seconds to subsecond without changing the scored graph.
task010 updated_v18 deletes the remaining `W[10]` by using inactive output
rows of an already-counted `R1[10,2]` table as scratch. The row sums of
scratch rows 5..9 carry the former coefficient contribution inside the final
`Einsum`, while their two components are split to keep wrong output channels
non-positive on the finite generator domain. Params drop `50 -> 40` at memory
0, but this relies on unused channel rows being truly inactive as outputs.

## `repeated-factor-coefficient-absorption` (absorb a small coefficient vector into an already-repeated Einsum factor)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A zero-memory direct-output `Einsum` multiplies a small
coefficient vector `D[q]` by several repeated copies of another learned factor
`U[..., q]`.  The coefficient is only used on the same latent axis and the
equation can tolerate one additional `U` operand summed over a row/basis axis.

**Recipe.** If the old product has `m` copies of `U[:, q]` and one `D[q]`,
replace `D` with one more `U` operand and rescale each column of `U`:

```python
alpha[q] = sign(D[q] / U[:, q].sum()) * abs(D[q] / U[:, q].sum()) ** (1 / (m + 1))
U_new[:, q] = alpha[q] * U_old[:, q]
```

Then change the scalar `q` operand to a summed row/basis operand such as
`bq`.  The `m` original factor uses contribute `alpha[q]**m`, and the new
row-summed factor contributes `sum_b U_old[b, q] * alpha[q]`, reproducing
`D[q]` without storing `D`.

**Why.** This deletes a small coefficient initializer without adding activation
memory or graph nodes.  It is most useful for fitted projective direct-output
`Einsum` renderers where initializer params dominate the score and a latent
axis already appears many times.

**Limits.** Requires nonzero `U[:, q].sum()` for every absorbed coefficient
and can change numeric margins.  Verify the emitted ONNX under the target ORT
version, especially when the original fitted graph had small true/false logit
margins.

**Tasks.** task336 updated_10 absorbs the old `D[3]` coefficient vector into
the already-repeated `U[2,3]` projective factor by adding an eleventh `U`
operand with equation label `bq`.  Params drop `89 -> 86`, memory remains
`0`, and required splits plus 100 extras pass.
task329 updated uses the same row-sum idea in a smaller coefficient core:
the separate `T[2,2]` matrix is replaced by another `D[h,f,g]` operand summed
over `g`, after retuning `CE` and `D` so the folded row sums preserve the
middle-column classifier margins.  Params drop `92 -> 88`, memory remains
`0`, and required splits plus 100 extras pass.
task106 updated_v6 uses the same absorption principle as a column-gauge
retune: a finite-domain search found `gate_coeff[g,p] = V[g,p] * W[p]`, then
rescales the shared `U/V/coeff` factors so the explicit gate coefficient
initializer disappears while the one-node graph-output `Einsum` stays exact on
the 2x2/3x3 generator domain. Params drop `182 -> 174`, memory remains `0`,
and required splits plus 100 extras pass.
task106 updated_v44 is a slow-variant extension: it synthesizes the former
`V3[2,2]` factor from repeated `V1` and diagonal `Gate**6` factors with a
global q selector, reducing the known 72-param variant to 68 params.  The
single arc-gen[0] smoke sample passed, but ORT estimated required-split
runtime above 7600s, so keep it as probe-only rather than a locally promoted
builder.
task329 updated_10 goes one step further by using unreachable coordinate
columns in the shared `CF[2,30]` table as a scratch bank that synthesizes both
the affine core `D[2,2,2]` and the coefficient matrix `T[2,2]` inside the
single output `Einsum`.  This deletes the explicit `D` initializer
(`88 -> 80` params, memory `0`).  The same algebra was slow with a local-groups
operand order, but moving the runtime cell earlier and delaying the T/spatial
row-summary groups kept the ORT contraction under the slow-variant threshold
while preserving all margins.
task148 updated_v9 applies the same delete-a-vector idea to a finite
TfIdf-driven portal renderer: two sign-preserving label merges let the final
output `Einsum` synthesize a positive multiple of the old `OBfac[2]` vector as
`sum_aG CA[a,G] * CB[G,l] = [4,1]`.  Because only output signs matter, the
global factor of four is harmless, and params drop `113 -> 111` with

task237 updated_v4 deletes the two-element `F0` coefficient vector by reusing

## `scale-migration-into-repeated-einsum-factors` (delete a scalar scale by compensating existing repeated factors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output or scalar-moment solver has a small scalar
scale initializer that appears only to preserve numeric magnitude for a
subsequent cast/quantization, and the same expression also contains repeated
small factors whose product can absorb that scale without changing the final
signs or integer-rounded payloads.

**Recipe.** Remove the scalar scale from the moment decoder and migrate its
effect into repeated factors already present in every dependent expression. If
the old expression was `C / s * J * J`, replace it with `C * (J / sqrt(s)) *
(J / sqrt(s))` or the equivalent inverse scaling, then switch the decoder from
`QuantizeLinear(..., y_scale=s)` to `Cast(..., UINT8)` only after checking that
the rounded finite-domain payloads are unchanged.  This is a sign-preserving
algebraic rewrite, not a numeric approximation; verify the emitted ONNX because
fp32 cancellation and ORT `Einsum` operand order can move tight margins.

**Why.** ONNX counts even one scalar initializer.  When the scalar can be
distributed into already-counted repeated factors, score improves without
adding memory or graph nodes.  It is most useful in packed moment decoders and
single-Einsum renderers where a previous scale was only a convenience for
integer extraction.

**Tasks.** task020 updated_v4 removes the explicit `base=1024` scalar from
the packed row/column decoder, replaces the two `QuantizeLinear(..., base)`
payload decoders with direct `Cast(UINT8)`, and scales the shared `Jm` factor
by 32 so the residual colour moments and final direct-output renderer remain
sign-equivalent. Cost improves `73/90 -> 72/90` and local score
`19.9062 -> 19.9124`; required splits and 100/100 extras pass.
task365 updated_v30 migrates a one-element underflow scale into four repeated
`NZ` factors in a zero-memory direct-output `Einsum`, deleting the scalar
initializer while preserving ORT 1.24.4 sign behavior. Cost improves
`996 -> 932` with 100/100 promotion extras.
task359's 2026-07-11 HF-confirmed graph is the complementary endpoint: instead
of deleting the last scalar, it replaces a four-byte `RandomUniform` scale
source with one explicit fp32 scalar and a higher-order self-`Einsum`, dropping
cost `4 -> 1` and reaching score `25.0`.  This is useful evidence that a
single counted scalar can beat a zero-param random source when the random
tensor's intermediate memory would be counted.

## `repeated-einsum-basis-only-fit` (collapse a fitted direct renderer into one initializer repeated many times in a single Einsum)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A direct-output Einsum renderer has several small factor
tables and dense cores, and the rule domain is small enough to fit a lower-cost
factorization offline. Instead of storing separate coordinate bases, channel
bases, and core tensors, try fitting one shared basis `E[k,N]` and referencing
it many times in the same Einsum equation. ONNX counts each initializer once,
so repeated references can delete many small tables even if the equation looks
large.

**Why this is a win.** task085 team port replaces a symbolic four-initializer
branch-factored punchcard renderer (`E[2,30]`, `H[2,2,2]`, `F[2,2,10]`,
`T[2,2,2,2]`, 124 params) with one fitted `E[2,30]` referenced 55+ times in
the final output Einsum. Cost drops `124 -> 60` at memory zero, with required
splits and 100/100 extras passing.
task072 team port applies the same repeated-basis compression to a
top/bottom-XOR row matcher: `C[30,2]`, `s[2]`, and `z[10]` are repeated 380
times inside one output Einsum, replacing the previous symbolic 74-param
projective renderer with a 72-param fitted graph. Required splits and 100/100
extras pass, but runtime is slower than the symbolic form.
task151 team port folds the old explicit coefficient core into repeated uses
of `B[2,30]`, `E[2,10]`, and one shared `T[2,2,2]` while preserving the
ORT-safe operand ordering. This reduces params `96 -> 88` at memory zero with
required splits and 100/100 extras passing, but remains a slow single-Einsum
solver (~48s required runtime locally).
The 2026-06-23 promoted team ONNX batch expands this family beyond the early
hand-tuned examples.  Single-output repeated-basis `Einsum` ports were
Kaggle-confirmed for task061, task110, task063, task320, task292, task375,
task188, task318, task236, task317, task072, task211, task093, task180,
task144, task081, task261, task058, task074, task084, task094, task099,
task086, task162, and task173.  Typical wins are `0/20 -> 0/10` on task061,
`0/80 -> 0/40` on task320, and `0/90 -> 0/68` on task188: the graph may look
like an enormous algebraic expression, but the counted artifact is just one
basis initializer referenced many times.
The 2026-06-24 HF leaderboard promotion added another confirmed retune layer
to the same family: task299 `0/20 -> 0/10`, task063 `0/24 -> 0/20`,
task292 `0/50 -> 0/40`, task211 `0/68 -> 0/62`, task294 `0/96 -> 0/88`,
task232 `0/116 -> 0/96`, task220 `0/130 -> 0/100`, and task099
`0/221 -> 0/211`.  These are mostly table-factor retunes rather than new
algorithms, but they are a good reminder to refit the already-good one-op
models after each new shared-basis trick.

**Caveats.** This is a fitted separator, not automatically an algorithmic
proof. Only use it when the fitted graph is verified on required splits plus
promotion extras, and prefer Kaggle probing before relying on a new family
whose generator admits broader cases than the local sample set.

## `dynamic-qzp-negative-index-scatter` (reuse a dynamic zero point as a negative scatter index and update)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A small generator-bounded task needs to route one runtime
class into a channel-specific `ConvInteger` weight and already has a packed
scalar containing both a count `N` and colour/class code `c`.

**Recipe.** Encode the packed scalar so the low byte casts to `N`, while
`QuantizeLinear(code, scale=256, zero_point=N)` emits a negative multiple such
as `-(10-c) * N`.  Divide by `N` to get a negative ONNX channel index
`c - 10`.  Use that same negative tensor both as the `ScatterElements` index
and as the signed update value into an int8 weight bank.  Negative indices
write to the desired channel, and the written negative value can drive a
`ConvInteger` threshold with dynamic `x_zero_point=N`.

**Why.** This can remove a one-element static update initializer and sometimes
a static quantize zero-point initializer.  It is only appropriate when the
class range is known, negative indices are accepted by the target ONNX op, and
only the sign or relative ordering of the scattered weight matters.

**Tasks.** task339 updated_9 reverses the packed colour/count code so
`QuantizeLinear` with dynamic zero point `N` emits `-(10-c)N`; after division,
`c-10` is reused as both negative scatter index and ConvInteger weight.  Local
promotion passed required splits plus 100/100 extras, reducing params
`31 -> 30` at the same 22-byte memory.

## `convinteger-xor-selected-channel-renderer` (BitwiseXor runtime colour id with channel id and clip the row factor)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task selects a few runtime colour ids, usually from
`TopK`, and renders solid columns/stripes/rectangles in those selected output
channels. The naive dynamic `ConvInteger` renderer builds an
`Equal(channel_id, selected_id)` mask plus `Where` or a separate column-valid
gate.

**Recipe.** Keep selected ids in `uint8`. Invalidate non-selected TopK slots
with a modular value such as `idx | (count - max_count)`, so max-count ties
stay legal ids and non-ties become impossible ids. Build the dynamic
ConvInteger weight as:

```python
w = BitwiseXor(channel_id_u8, selected_id_u8)
ConvInteger(row_factor_u8, w, x_zero_point=threshold, w_zero_point=1)
```

XOR is zero on the selected output channel. With `w_zero_point=1`, selected
weights have effective value `-1`, adjacent wrong channels have `0`, and other
wrong channels are positive. If wrong-channel positives can leak into inactive
rows, clamp the row factor to the runtime threshold first, for example
`row_factor = Min(static_rows, max_count)`, so inactive rows have zero
effective input.

**Rejected opset14 arithmetic probe.** If bitwise ops force opset18 and cost an
axes initializer elsewhere, it is tempting to use uint8 arithmetic instead:

```python
idxv = Max(idx_u8, count - max_count)  # legal id or wrapped 254/255/...
w = Sub(channel_id_u8, idxv)           # zero exactly on selected channel
```

The same `w_zero_point=1` sign logic appears to apply, while opset14 lets
ReduceMax use attribute axes.  In task247 this passed train/test/arc-gen plus
100/100 extras and cut cost `195 -> 192`, but Kaggle returned `0.00`.  Treat
this arithmetic rewrite as a risky-probe/anti-pattern until individually
confirmed on another task; keep the opset18 BitwiseXor form as the safe current
technique.

**Why.** This replaces a dynamic bool equality tensor and a `Where`-built
weight bank with one bitwise op, and the uint8 wraparound invalidation can
delete a separate tie mask. It is especially useful when the final
ConvInteger already pads a compact row/column factor directly to the 30x30
scorer canvas.

**Limits.** The XOR form requires opset 18 bitwise ops. Check the sign margins:
wrong-channel positive weights must be neutralized by the input factor or kept
below the selected channel logits.  Do not replace XOR with modular `Sub`
solely to lower opset/cost unless the exact task variant is probed.

**Tasks.** task247 updated_8 uses `BitwiseOr(idx, count-max_count)` for
TopK-slot invalidation and `BitwiseXor(channel_id, idx)` as the dynamic
ConvInteger weight. Clamping `rows0` with `Min(rows0, max_count)` prevents
wrong-channel leaks below the rectangle. Kaggle confirmed this recovery at
public score 19.72 after v10 failed, reducing cost `216 -> 195`.
task247 updated_10 switched the same renderer to opset14 arithmetic:
`Max(idx, count-max_count)` invalidates non-max slots and
`Sub(channel_id, idx)` builds the dynamic ConvInteger weights. Dropping opset18
deleted the one-element ReduceMax axes initializer and cut cost `195 -> 192`,
but Kaggle returned `0.00`; this is a rejected probe despite local required
splits plus 100/100 extras passing.

## `signless-orientation-probe` (sample binary taps so a-b is already the orientation sign)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A finite-geometry task needs a small orientation or
row/column relation flag from two probe cells, and the previous graph samples
colour-coded values then applies `Sign(a-b)` to collapse arbitrary differences
to `-1/0/+1`.

**Recipe.** If an existing colour-code basis has a homogeneous/nonblack tap,
sample that tap instead of the full colour value. Arrange the tap so black or
background casts to `0`, while every relevant nonblack probe casts to `1`.
Then:

```python
ConvTranspose(input, binary_tap) -> a32, b32
Cast(a32), Cast(b32) -> a8, b8
Sub(a8, b8) -> orientation
```

The subtraction is already in `{-1,0,+1}` for valid probes, so the `Sign`
intermediate and its counted output byte can be deleted. If the same basis is
also used downstream as a colour code, tune only the homogeneous coefficient
slightly, for example `0.999999`, so integer cast sees black as `0` while the
fp32 code remains close enough for the final classifier.

**Why.** This is a small but clean cost cut in direct-renderer graphs where
orientation feeds dynamic offsets. It is safer than fitting a new orientation
classifier because it preserves the exact valid-domain binary predicate and
only removes a redundant normalization op.

**Limits.** Only use when the two sampled values are guaranteed binary on
train/test/arc-gen and generator-valid hidden cases. If probe values can be
multi-level, keep `Sign` or an explicit comparator.

**Tasks.** task107 fast_v3 samples the existing `F2[...,0]` homogeneous tap
for the two 2x2-box probes, sets black to `0.999999`, then casts to int8 and
uses `rv8-cv8` directly. This removes the `Sign` node from the direct-output
Einsum renderer and reduces cost `449 -> 446` (`18.8930 -> 18.8997` local)
while passing train/test/arc-gen plus 100/100 extras.
task107 fast_v9 multiplies the signless orientation moment by the runtime
scale factor before the cast, using a free scalar synthesized from existing
`Bs2/Sneg/R1` factors.  `Cast(INT8)` now emits `f * orientation` directly,
and `4*f - abs(d8)` recovers the companion offset.  This deletes the separate
orientation byte and multiply output, reducing cost `421 -> 420` with 100/100
extras.

## `count-moment-factor-decoder` (decode a small scale/factor from all-channel count moments)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A generator-valid input has a fixed total mass plus a small
number of variable colour partitions, and an existing graph probes several
individual side colours only to recover a small runtime factor such as scale,
repeat count, or palette count.

**Recipe.** Replace the per-colour probes with global count moments:

```python
s2 = Einsum(input, input, coef2, equation="nchw,ncij,z->n")
s3 = Einsum(input, input, input, coef3, equation="nchw,ncij,nckl,z->n")
factor = Cast(s2 + s3 + bias, INT8)
```

Fit the affine separator on `(sum count_c^2, sum count_c^3)` over the generator
domain with enough margin before integer truncation or rounding.  This is often
cheaper than carrying one probe per possible side/palette colour.

**Why.** Count moments are scalar and ignore spatial layout, which is exactly
what scale/palette-count decoders need.  They can delete several
ConvTranspose/Equal/Cast/Add probes when the generator fixes the background,
box, and total side-cell counts.

**Limits.** This is a fitted finite-domain decoder.  It is safe only when the
generator constrains the colour-count multiset tightly and the fitted margins
are checked on train/test/arc-gen plus diagnostics.  Do not use it for tasks
where hidden cases can introduce unseen count partitions.

**Tasks.** task107 fast_v5 replaces five scalar side-colour probes with
second/third count moments to recover the magnification factor, cutting cost
`446 -> 429` (`18.8997 -> 18.9385` local) with 100/100 extras.

**Scalar-coefficient fold.** task107 fast_v7 deletes the two one-element
moment coefficient initializers by synthesizing them inside the S2/S3
`Einsum`s from existing renderer constants (`Bs2`, `R1`, and `Sneg`) and
retuning the bias. This is useful when a graph already stores small matrices
whose full contraction equals the needed scalar. It reduces params `129 -> 127`
with unchanged memory, moving local score `18.9503 -> 18.9550`.
task107 fast_v10 pushes the remaining factor bias into generator-safe scratch
values stored in the unused last column of the Resize source table.  The S2/S3
moment contractions multiply by reductions of that scratch column, and the
constant bias becomes `four8 * four8`.  The same scratch column synthesizes the
orientation amplifier, deleting the final scalar bias initializer and reducing
params `127 -> 126` with unchanged memory and 100/100 extras.

## `shared-lagrange-root-retune` (retune one polynomial root so adjacent selectors share an initializer)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output polynomial renderer stores several small
Lagrange/root factors for adjacent lattice selectors, and two selectors have a
common zero/root after a harmless reparameterization.

**Recipe.** Retune the selector factors so one root row is valid for both
branches, then reference the same initializer in each branch of the final
Einsum.  Fold any deleted scalar multipliers into the remaining class or
selector table.

**Why.** In high-arity direct-output Einsums, deleting a two-element root vector
can still improve score, and reusing an existing initializer is free when the
same value name appears multiple times in the node input list.

**Limits.** Re-solve the products exactly on every legal lattice line.  This is
not a numerical approximation unless the task already uses a fitted classifier.

**Tasks.** task185 fast_v5 retunes `f0r0` to share one root between the
top-corner and bottom-corner selectors and folds the final scalar into
`class_v`, reducing params `129 -> 127` (`19.1594 -> 19.1652` local).

## `selector-gauge-reuse` (reorder bases so one selector table serves multiple roles)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output Einsum carries separate selector matrices for
channel summaries and coordinate summaries, but both selectors choose the same
logical lanes after basis reordering.

**Recipe.** Gauge-reorder the small bases so the desired rows line up, then use
one selector initializer with different index names in the same Einsum.  Combine
this with repeated value-name inputs when a period or root projection is needed
more than once; the scorer counts the initializer only once.

**Why.** Basis reordering is free in the algebra but can delete entire selector
tables.  This is especially effective in one-node direct renderers where graph
memory is already zero and the score is dominated by initializer elements.

**Limits.** Verify the reordered bases preserve all sign margins and colour
separators.  Repeated input names are safe, but the equation labels must still
keep the intended tensor axes independent.

**Tasks.** task358 fast_v13 reorders the channel/coordinate bases so `SEL`
replaces separate `SLC`/`SLP` selectors and reuses `Q0` for repeated period
projections, reducing params `327 -> 237` (`19.2100 -> 19.5319` local).
task273 v4 rescales a rank factor so `diag(Bfac)` becomes the yellow-channel
selector, deleting a separate 2-entry `V` vector and reducing cost
`102 -> 100` (`20.3750 -> 20.3948` local).  task099 updated_v1 absorbs the
`WL[2,2]` coordinate transform into `U`, `W`, and `L2` while preserving the
row-sum constraints used by the one-node renderer, deleting four params at
zero memory cost (`210 -> 206`) with required splits plus 100/100 extras
passing.  task099 updated_v3 goes one step further: the old `W[3,2]` selector
is synthesized inside the final `Einsum` as `RHw @ L2 @ Rmat`, with the
per-row projective scale absorbed into the qx3 coefficient matrices, reducing
params `206 -> 204` while keeping memory zero and passing required splits plus
100/100 extras.  task099 updated_v7 deletes the remaining `Rmat[2,2]` by
solving a row scale that makes `RHw @ L2` projectively parallel to the old
`RHw @ L2 @ Rmat` coordinate roots, then compensating the per-selector scales
in the repeated quadratic coefficient tables; params drop `204 -> 200` with
memory still zero and 100/100 extras passing.  task099 updated_v8 deletes the
dense `Tgeo[5,2]` gate table by synthesizing its two live rows from already
stored factors: `(RWw @ tc) * (L2 @ TgM)`.  The support vector is exact on the

task099 updated_v9 then uses unreachable coordinate rows in the existing
`U[30,2]` table as scratch to synthesize the remaining `TgM[2,2]` transform

task163 updated_v2 diagonally
scales the shared channel code
so the yellow row equals the old two-element `B` vector; because a yellow

## `epsilon-lane-underflow-fold` (replace a stored mask lane with epsilon leakage below output threshold)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct renderer stores a tiny mask or residue table only
to block leakage from an otherwise useful lane, and the final output already
uses a very small positive/negative mask with `output > 0` semantics.

**Recipe.** Retune the auxiliary lane to `+/-eps`, rescale only the branch that
needs the real feature back to its original magnitude, and let all other uses
see only epsilon-sized leakage.  Choose `eps` so the leaked term remains below
the final signed-logit threshold margin after every downstream multiplier.

**Why.** This can delete a small mask initializer without changing the branch
that really needs the feature.  It is useful in modular/phase renderers where a
parity lane is consumed by one factor but should be invisible to another.

**Limits.** This is a numerical margin technique.  Verify with ONNX Runtime and
avoid it when hidden inputs can shrink sign margins or when the target branch
uses integer casts that would erase the epsilon lane.

**Tasks.** task014 fast_v9 retunes the parity lane in `Code4` to `+/-1e-8` and
rescales `ParMap`, deleting the explicit four-entry `ModMask` initializer.
Cost drops `389 -> 385` (`19.0364 -> 19.0468` local) with 100/100 extras.

## `moment-orientation-decoder` (recover orientation from a signed coordinate moment instead of probe tensors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task needs a small orientation sign and generator symmetry
makes all distractor contributions cancel under a signed coordinate moment.

**Recipe.** Replace explicit probe/scalar tensors with one global moment such
as `sum color * (col-row)`.  If all symmetric side colours cancel and only the
object of interest contributes, cast/sign that scalar to recover `-1/0/+1`.

**Why.** A scalar moment can delete multiple spatial probes and their cast/sub
chain while preserving the same orientation signal.

**Limits.** Requires a real generator invariant.  If distractors are not
perfectly mirrored or the contributing colour can be zero, keep direct probes.

**Tasks.** task107 fast_v6 replaces the two 2x2-box ConvTranspose orientation
probes with a diagonal signed colour moment, cutting memory `300 -> 295`
(`18.9385 -> 18.9503` local) with 100/100 extras.

## `fixed-pixel-runtime-colour-gate` (use a guaranteed separator pixel to avoid full colour-count vectors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The generator guarantees that one coordinate is always a
runtime role colour, for example a separator or line colour, and that coordinate
is never overwritten by later stamps.

**Recipe.** Crop/probe that fixed pixel and build a small channel gate such as
`not black and not line_colour` directly from it.  Combine this with total and
nonblack scalar counts when the old graph carried a full per-channel population
vector only to infer the same runtime state.

**Why.** Fixed-role pixels are cheaper than dynamic colour histograms.  A
grouped 1x1 convolution or compact pixel crop can delete per-channel count,
ReduceMax, and activation-normalization tensors.

**Limits.** Only safe when the fixed coordinate is invariant across generator
and hidden cases.  If any case can move or overwrite the role pixel, keep the
histogram or a robust marker detector.

**Tasks.** task185 fast_v6 uses fixed pixel `(14,3)` as the runtime line colour
and black count as the lattice-step decoder, reducing cost `342 -> 330`
(`19.1652 -> 19.2009` local) with 100/100 extras.  task185 v10 keeps that
fixed-pixel gate and retunes the shared gate amplitude so `q126` is both the
final QLinearConv threshold scale and the lattice-step QuantizeLinear scale;
the coordinate basis is rescaled so `pow_exp=1/50` also serves as the
row/column quantizer scale, dropping params `139 -> 137`.

## `p-independent-period-root` (delete a period axis when a root can be shared across cases)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A one-node direct renderer stores period/case-specific root
vectors, but search or algebra shows one root value separates all relevant
period cases with the same sign margins.

**Recipe.** Retune the root to a shared scalar/vector, remove the period label
from that factor's Einsum term, and keep the remaining period-specific roots
explicit.  This is a small but reliable initializer reduction when the graph is
already memory-zero and parameter dominated.

**Why.** Removing one case axis from a root table deletes all entries along
that axis and often has no runtime cost.

**Limits.** Recheck sign margins on all required/generated cases; this is often
a fitted separator rather than an exact algebraic identity.

**Tasks.** task358 fast_v14 retunes `Q2` to one p-independent root, reducing
params `237 -> 233` (`19.5319 -> 19.5490` local) with 100/100 extras.

## `unit-homogeneous-band-factor` (emit repeated smooth relation bands by reusing coordinate tables)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A cyclic or polynomial relation contains a repeated smooth
band such as `1 + cos(i-j)` and the existing graph stores a coefficient table
only to form that homogeneous dot product.

**Recipe.** Choose a coordinate basis `F` where the desired band is exactly
`F[i,a] * F[j,a]` under an Einsum repeated label, then reuse the same table
twice instead of storing a separate band coefficient initializer.  If the final
core is also low-rank, fold correction magnitudes into nearby band weights and
replace dense `Core[p,t]` with small factors such as `C[p,t] * T[t]`.

**Why.** Repeated value-name inputs and repeated labels are free in scorer
params when they reuse the same initializer.  This is especially useful for
direct-output cyclic renderers where memory is already zero or tiny.

**Limits.** This often increases local runtime because the final Einsum becomes
more algebraically factored.  Smoke-test first and save as a slow variant if it
exceeds the promotion gate.

**Tasks.** task265 fast_v17 emits the smooth band from repeated `F` factors and
factorizes the core/correction path, improving the slow-variant frontier from
`mem=24, params=149` to `mem=24, params=140` (`19.8467 -> 19.9001` local) but
with estimated required runtime around 218s, so it is saved for probing.

## `einsum-unit-root-and-lane-scale-fold` (delete coefficient operands that are algebraically all-ones and fold lane normalizers into roots)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output Fourier/CRT or cyclic-root renderer carries
tiny coefficient vectors only to multiply one lane by 1, or carries a separate
normalizer whose lanes are consumed by disjoint lanes of an angle-add/root
core.

**Recipe.** If a coefficient vector is exactly all ones over the shared
Einsum label, omit that operand and label entirely; an absent coefficient is
the same multiplicative identity.  If a normalizer has lane-wise scales and
the downstream core routes each lane independently, multiply those scales into
the root/phase vector and delete the normalizer operand.  Recompute the final
operand order after deletion, because ORT contracts `Einsum` mostly
left-to-right.

**Why.** This is a pure params reduction for memory-zero or near-zero direct
renderers.  It is especially useful after a manual-protobuf rewrite where
initializer count dominates and repeated input names are free.

**Limits.** Only exact when the removed vector is truly the multiplicative
identity or when core sparsity guarantees lane-disjoint scaling.  If lanes mix,
the scale fold changes the relation.  Verify under ORT and keep the runtime
operand order compact.

**Tasks.** task400 updated_v9 folds `Norm3=[0.04,0.2,0.2]` into `P3` because
the angle-add core routes lane 0 separately from trig lanes, and deletes
`R8_3=[1,1,1]` by omitting the all-ones coefficient operand.  Params drop
`274 -> 268`, memory stays `12`, required splits plus 100/100 promotion extras
pass, and the reordered manual-protobuf graph keeps required runtime around
5.8s locally.  task035 updated_v4 applies the same identity-operand deletion
through a diagonal tensor-network gauge: the `R0` vector becomes all ones, so
its two final-Einsum operands are removed and the remaining lane scales are
folded into the shared `Gate`/`S` roots.  updated_v6 then stores the former
`R1[0]` coefficient on `Rright[0,0]` and reads the diagonal labels (`ss`,
`UU`) instead of carrying a separate `R1[2]` initializer.  Params drop
`146 -> 142`.  updated_v8 pushes the same idea further by synthesizing
`Rright` and the former `R1` from already-counted `Rbottom`/`G` scratch
diagonals and factoring `S` into `D * Bs * Rbottom^3 * G`.  Final params drop
`146 -> 135`, memory stays `16`, and required splits plus 100/100 extras pass.

## `custom-3lane-color-halfspace` (pack colors into a small homogeneous trig code so one shared code supplies identity, stamp, and black-window tests)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output `Einsum` needs one channel embedding to do
several jobs at once: preserve same-color identity, isolate one output color
for a stamp, and score whether local windows are all black versus
black-plus-foreground.  The input palette is restricted enough that foreground
colors can be packed into one arc away from black/blue.

**Recipe.** Use a 3-lane homogeneous trig code `E[c] = [1, cos(theta_c),
sin(theta_c)]`, but choose angles for the task rather than equally spacing all
10 colors.  Put black and the stamp color at convenient halfspace normals, and
pack all legal foreground colors into a far arc where the black halfspace has a
small bounded response.  Reuse the same `E` table for output logits and local
window features; if a second local factor only needs occupancy, replace its
channel table with a scalar state vector over `sum_c input[c,r,w]`.

**Why.** This can delete one embedding lane and one local feature matrix in
already-tiny direct renderers.  It is also a way to make a black-window
underflow detector robust without storing separate foreground masks.

**Limits.** The angle packing is task-distribution dependent.  Recheck all
legal foreground colors and the exact zero-margin cases under ORT fp32; this is
best for generators with known palette exclusions.

**Tasks.** task162 v26 replaces a 4-lane `E/P/H` design with a 3-lane
homogeneous/cos/sin code and a scalar second local factor, reducing
`mem=8, params=411` to `mem=8, params=399` while passing required splits and
100/100 promotion extras.  task162 v28 deletes the scalar `J` factor by
rescaling `H1` so `sum_feat H1[t, feat]` supplies the deleted state scale, and
uses `GatherElements(axis=3)` for the single guard cell instead of a 4-index
`GatherND`, reducing params `399 -> 395`.

## `synthesize-metric-from-counted-einsum-operands` (replace a small transform table with a derived metric built from already-counted operands)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A final direct-output `Einsum` has a tiny transform,
diagonal, or metric table used only to weight a short feature axis, and the
graph already includes small counted operands that can algebraically generate
the same metric.

**Recipe.** Express the metric as an extra leading contraction over operands
already present in the final `Einsum`, for example
`D[q] = einsum('qLJ,qMK,KJ,KK,JL,ML,JM->q', ...)`.  Place that tiny derived
metric prefix before the large spatial operands so ONNX Runtime contracts the
small factors first.  Then remove the explicit transform initializer and wire
the downstream channel features directly through the derived `q` weight.

**Why.** Repeated use of an existing initializer does not add params, while the
deleted transform table does.  This is a pure cost reduction for
memory-zero/direct-renderer graphs when the algebra is exact.

**Limits.** Operand order matters for runtime.  Smoke-test the rewritten
Einsum, because algebraically equivalent equations can be much slower if ORT
contracts a large spatial factor before the tiny metric.

**Tasks.** task169 v5 removes the 3x3 current-cell transform `T` by deriving
`D=[1.5,1.0,-0.5]` from existing `Grel/LC` operands placed first in the final
Einsum, reducing `mem=0, params=265` to `mem=0, params=256` with 100/100
promotion extras.

## `quantizelinear-dynamic-zero-point-frame-fold` (use runtime zero point to align two decoded coordinates and delete an explicit scale term)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** Two runtime coordinate decoders are naturally in different
frames, and the downstream rule only needs their difference or relative offset.
A naive graph materializes an explicit scale/size product to translate one
coordinate before subtracting.

**Recipe.** Set the `QuantizeLinear` zero point of one decoder to the runtime
frame offset, so the quantized result is already shifted into the other
decoder's coordinate frame.  Then compute the relative coordinate with one
`Sub` and delete the explicit `scale * size`, `Add`, or frame-normalization
byte.

**Why.** `QuantizeLinear` zero point is an input and may be runtime-derived.
If the valid generator states make both decoders integral and aligned after the
zero-point shift, the zero point acts as a free affine frame translation.

**Limits.** Only safe when the shifted decoder remains in-range for the chosen
quantized dtype and round-to-nearest exactly recovers the desired integer for
all required states.  Smoke-test because a dynamic zero point can hide a frame
mistake until a rare size/scale combination appears.

**Tasks.** task170 updated_v2 decodes `big_last_col_u8` with dynamic zero point
`size_u8`; subtracting `visible_plus_u8` then yields the magnified sprite sample
column directly.  This deletes the materialized `big_w_u8 = scale * size`,
reducing memory `447 -> 446` with params unchanged and 100/100 promotion extras.
task170 updated_v4 removes the separate row-12 scale probe: decode sprite scale
from a single inverted row-14 probe, use that same decoded scale as the sampler
start, and keep the existing fused `QLinearConv` classify-and-pad output tail.
Memory drops `446 -> 439` at unchanged params, with required splits and
100/100 extras passing.

## `stable-square-basis-quadratic-compaction` (replace [1,d,d,d²] product slots with constant plus shifted squares)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct-output `Einsum` represents a bounded
quadratic row/column relation with product features like `[1, d, d, d^2]`, but
one product slot is unused or numerically fragile.  The relation only needs the
span of quadratics, not that exact monomial basis.

**Recipe.** Reparameterize the relation in a three-feature basis such as
`[1, (d-a)^2, (d+a)^2]`.  Fit or solve the small coefficient tensor in that
basis, keeping the constant feature explicit so cancellation does not rely on
subtracting nearly equal large shifted-square terms.  Replace the old 2x2 core
with the smaller feature core and adjust the relation tensor accordingly.

**Why.** The shifted-square basis spans every quadratic while often using fewer
initializer elements than a product-core representation.  It can also be more
stable than a lower-param probe that derives the constant term from square
cancellations.

**Limits.** This is a pure algebraic refactor only when the finite domain is
covered by the new basis and all logits keep their sign margins in fp32.  Avoid
choosing shifts that make correct and incorrect classes nearly tie.

**Tasks.** task199 updated_v2 replaces the previous 2x2 row-product core with
`[1, (d-2)^2, (d+2)^2]`; the row core drops `32 -> 24` elements while the row
relation grows `8 -> 12`, for net `params 230 -> 226`, memory 0, and 100/100
promotion extras.  task199 updated_v5 moves marker and output colour roles
onto one shared rank-4 table `E`, using a 10-entry marker gate to suppress
black/yellow on the marker operand and normalizing shifted row/column distance
features; cost drops `222 -> 200`.  task199 updated_v7 folds the remaining
4-entry marker-gate vector into the shared colour table itself: store
`E = diag(W) E0`, divide `J` by `W^2`, and use the row sum `sum_g E[g,d]` as
the marker gate inside the same output `Einsum`.  This removes the separate
gate initializer, reducing cost `200 -> 190` with required splits plus 100/100
extras passing.
task199 updated_v9 then deletes the explicit `B[2,3]` coordinate-projection
initializer by using unreachable `X[:,15:29]` coordinate columns as algebraic
scratch, together with the already-counted `CLd` tensor, to synthesize
`B[U,u]` inline inside the final output `Einsum`.  This is slow locally but
Kaggle-confirmed in the 2026-06-30 excluded-task batch; cost improves
`190 -> 184` at memory `0`.  task199 updated_v11 retunes those unreachable
`X` columns so their row sums project `[1, coord, parity]` down to
`[1, coord]`, then uses the same `CLd` scratch table to synthesize the shifted
row mixer inside the final `Einsum`; this deletes the remaining `M/RS` row
mixing tables, reducing cost `184 -> 172` with memory `0`, 100/100 extras, and
required runtime around 9.1s locally.

## `bitfield-transition-root-renderer` (pack ordered events into one integer, diff with XOR/BitShift, then render from roots)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task depends on the ordered transition pattern of a
sparse 1-D event sequence, such as the starts/ends of coloured runs or
segments, and a direct renderer only needs the transition bits and a few
derived scalar offsets.  A naive graph materializes per-event masks, one-hot
run states, or several explicit transition probes.

**Recipe.** Use an `Einsum` with powers-of-two weights to pack the event
presence sequence into one integer-like scalar.  Quantize/divide by the
runtime offset if needed, then compute transition bits as
`trans = rel XOR (rel << 1)`.  Extract low bits with repeated
`BitShift`/`BitwiseAnd`, turn each active bit into a small root/state vector,
and feed those root vectors directly into the final output `Einsum`.

**Why.** The bitfield carries many ordered boolean decisions through one tiny
runtime scalar instead of several masks.  The transition extraction ops are
cheap compared with carrying full row/column grids, and the final renderer can
reuse the same root/core tables across every decoded bit.

**Limits.** Keep the packed width inside the exact integer range used by the
chosen dtype/operation path.  fp32 mantissa only gives 24 exact bits, and
uint8/BitShift paths wrap or truncate.  This is best for generator-bounded
event counts where every extracted bit has a verified sign margin.

**Tasks.** task148 team port packs cyan event positions with a powers-of-two
axis vector, shifts by the recovered start offset, computes transition bits
with `BitwiseXor(rel, rel << 1)`, extracts seven event/root lanes, and renders
through one high-arity direct-output `Einsum`.  The 2026-06-24 HF leaderboard
retune keeps the bitfield transition renderer but rewrites the event-lane
decode from repeated subtract/cast/Where tests into compact Add/BitShift
lanes.  Memory/params improve `185/199 -> 129/154`, cost `384 -> 283`, and
score `19.0494 -> 19.3546`.

## `whole-pipeline-direct-einsum-collapse` (collapse detector/crop/classifier pipelines into one graph-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A solver first builds a compact finite state with
`ConvTranspose`, `QLinearConv`, `ConvInteger`, `MaxPool`, `Slice`,
`GatherElements`, `Equal`, or `Where`, then renders a full output from that
state.  If the generator domain is finite and the final mapping can be
represented by multilinear factors of input, coordinates, channel codes, and
small roots, the whole pipeline may be cheaper as one direct output
contraction.

**Recipe.** Replace each detected state bit, crop relation, or classifier
case with a factor in a single output `Einsum`.  Reuse coordinate/channel
basis tables many times inside the equation, and let the graph output be
signed logits directly.  It is acceptable for params to rise if the deleted
intermediates were full-canvas or multi-stage detector tensors.

**Why.** The scorer ignores the output tensor itself.  Trading a few hundred
more static parameters for removing hundreds or thousands of counted
intermediate bytes can dominate any micro-optimization of the original
pipeline.

**Limits.** This is a fitted high-arity graph unless the factorization is
derived from the generator.  It can be slow, and a small margin error usually
means the entire task scores zero.  Prefer Kaggle-confirmed ONNX, 100-extra
diagnostics, or a targeted probe before treating a new collapse as safe.

**Tasks.** task397 latest HF leaderboard port collapses an old
`ConvTranspose + 3 QLinearConv + ConvInteger + 4 MaxPool + GatherElements +
Equal + Where` graph to one `Einsum`: memory `1188 -> 0`, params
`108 -> 424`, cost `1296 -> 424`, score `17.8330 -> 18.9503`.
task075 collapses `ConvTranspose + Slice + 3 QLinearConv + Cast/Mul/Concat`
to one `Einsum`: memory `549 -> 0`, params `57 -> 270`, cost `606 -> 270`,
score `18.5931 -> 19.4016`.  The 2026-06-30 batch added smaller but useful
collapses: task048 keeps only scalar evidence `Einsum`s plus a final padded
`Conv`, reducing cost `289 -> 263`; task226 computes row/column moments and a
one-lane concat before the final renderer, reducing `355 -> 323`; task031
collapses the bbox/crop chain into log-quantized scalar decoders feeding one
renderer, reducing `403 -> 231`; task002 uses a tiny role predecoder before
the renderer and is documented separately.
