## `homogeneous-moment-root-decoder` (replace Mod/Div geometry grids with Fourier/root moment contractions)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A geometry-heavy solver materializes coordinate grids,
`Mod`/`Div` decompositions, or local scanner planes to decode a small finite
state such as phase, orientation, offset, or a pair relation.  The same state
can often be recovered from a few global or pairwise moments over the one-hot
input and fixed root/phase tables.

**Recipe.** Build compact coordinate/root tables and project the input through
several small `Einsum` contractions to obtain scalar moments.  Decode the
finite state with a tiny `MatMul`, `Gather`, or quantized tail, then expand to
the canvas only at the final classifier/renderer.  Keep moment tensors
scalar or short-vector sized; do not broadcast phase grids just to recreate a
procedural `Mod`/`Div` implementation.

**Why.** Root moments trade static parameters for deleting large intermediate
planes and arithmetic chains.  This is especially good when a codegolf
solution used modular arithmetic because it was short Python, while ONNX pays
memory for every decoded grid.

**Limits.** Moment separability must cover the legal generator domain, not
just the visible samples.  Check fp32 margins and degenerate symmetries; if
two states share the same low-order moments, add one more moment instead of
relying on accidental sample coverage.

**Tasks.** task264 HF leaderboard port replaces `Conv + MaxPool + ReduceSum +
7 Mod + 7 Div + 9 Mul + QLinearConv` with eight small moment `Einsum`
contractions, a `MatMul`, and a compact `QLinearConv` tail.  Memory/params
change `1140/205 -> 293/322`, cost `1345 -> 615`, and score
`17.7959 -> 18.5784`.
task264 updated_v4 further deletes 3-element root initializers by rewriting
some root vectors as products or powers of already-stored homogeneous roots:
`R4 ~= R6**8`, `R5` as a fifth power of inactive rows in the shared `F` table,
plus earlier `R2 ~= R1*R5` and `R3 ~= R1**3*R4*R6*R7`.  This is safe only
when the legal finite-state margins are explicitly checked; for task264 it
reduces params `238 -> 232` at memory 243, score `18.8241 -> 18.8367`, with
required splits and 100/100 extras passing.
task264 updated_v5 replaces the remaining `R1/R6` pair with powers of one
shared homogeneous base vector `B = [-t, 1, 1]` and folds the final
`QLinearConv` tail scale into the shared quantization scale plus scaled
`QCODE`.  The graph is slow enough to require targeted batch confirmation,
but Kaggle accepted it on 2026-06-30; cost improves `473 -> 471`
(`242/231 -> 243/228`) and score improves `18.8409 -> 18.8451`.

## `one-op-direct-output-port` (Kaggle-confirmed team ONNX collapses entire rule into one Einsum or ConvTranspose output)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A team ONNX, fitted renderer, or rewritten algorithm can
make the graph output directly from the original input plus a few static
factors.  The rule may be "complex" procedurally, but the legal generator
domain is small enough that the final mapping is a multilinear separator or a
single static-shape transposed-conv stamp.

**Recipe.** Inspect high-scoring ONNX candidates for graphs with exactly one
real compute op, usually `Einsum` or `ConvTranspose`, and no internal
activation that the scorer can count.  Port them literally into a Python
builder: one initializer table may be referenced many times in an `Einsum`
equation, and ONNX counts that initializer once.  Keep the output tensor as
the graph output, preferably logits, so the memory term is zero.

**Why.** Under the current `memory + params` scorer, deleting all intermediate
tensors is often worth more than keeping an interpretable multi-step graph.
The best cases also delete multiple small coefficient/core tables by repeating
one basis in the final contraction.

**Limits.** This is safest when the ONNX came from a Kaggle-confirmed batch or
when the factorization is derived over the full generator domain.  High-arity
`Einsum` can be slow even at memory zero, so smoke-test runtime and preserve a
faster same-score version if one exists.  Do not assume a fitted one-op graph
generalizes if extras expose states outside train/test/arc-gen.

**Tasks.** The 2026-06-23 promoted team batch confirmed 25 one-`Einsum`
memory-zero ports: task061, task110, task063, task320, task292, task375,
task188, task318, task236, task317, task072, task211, task093, task180,
task144, task081, task261, task058, task074, task084, task094, task099,
task086, task162, and task173.  It also confirmed one-`ConvTranspose` direct
ports for task164, task172, task210, task311, and task116.  Representative
cost drops: task061 `20 -> 10`, task320 `80 -> 40`, task188 `90 -> 68`, and
task164 `30 -> 16`.
The 2026-06-24 team promotion added another set of exact direct-output ports:
one-`Einsum` task026, task055, task125, task154, and task194, plus
one-`ConvTranspose` task053, task296, and task322.  task194 is the clearest
"repeat two tiny factors many times" example: one 2x30 coordinate/root table
and one 2-lane coefficient vector are reused hundreds of times in a single
Einsum, so counted params are only `62` while the output stays memory zero.
The 2026-06-24 HF leaderboard promotion then confirmed another wave of
direct-output ports and retunes: task397, task075, task299, task063, task292,
task211, task294, task232, task220, task154, task221, task156, and task099
all keep memory at zero or remove it entirely.  The largest wins are the

## `role-conv-predecode-direct-einsum` (use a tiny ReduceSum+Conv role map before the final direct-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct output renderer is available, but the legal cases
need a small global role/state code that is cheaper to decode explicitly than
to fold into a huge repeated-input `Einsum`.

**Recipe.** Reduce the one-hot input to a short global signature, run a tiny
static `Conv`/linear classifier over that signature to get role logits, and
feed those role logits into the final direct-output `Einsum`:

```python
ReduceSum(input, axes=[1, 2]) -> active_by_col_or_axis
Conv(active_by_col_or_axis, role_weight) -> roles
Einsum(input, roles, roles, coordinate_factors, ...) -> output
```

Keep the role tensor short and statically shaped.  The final output should
still be logits, so the renderer output itself is uncounted.

**Why.** A tiny predecoder can replace hundreds of repeated input references
or large case tables inside the renderer while avoiding full-canvas
intermediates.  This is especially useful when the rule has a few symbolic
roles that are clear from global occupancy or column/row signatures.

**Limits.** The role classifier must be exact for the generator domain.  Do
not turn this into a sampled shortcut unless the candidate is explicitly
treated as risky and probed.

**Tasks.** task002's 2026-06-30 team port uses
`ReduceSum(input, axes=[1,2]) -> Conv(WRoles) -> Roles`, then a high-arity
direct renderer with band and seed factors.  It replaced a 639-node
bitwise/prefix graph with three nodes, improving cost `3935 -> 1294` and score
`16.7221 -> 17.8343`.  task002 updated_v2 is a probe-confirmed narrower
variant: because legal Kaggle cases use dense top-left squares, the active
column mask is recovered from row 0 alone by `Conv(input, WTop)` with negative
bottom padding to crop height 30 to 1. This cuts memory at the cost of a larger
colour-aware role kernel (`360/934 -> 240/988`, score `17.8345 -> 17.8869`).
It passes train/test/arc-gen but only 93/100 cached extras, so treat similar
top-row-only shortcuts as risky/probe-before-promote unless individually
confirmed.
task002 updated_v3 is the next probe-confirmed refinement.  If one role is just
"constant 1 on every legal column", produce it with a legal full Conv bias
instead of a dynamic active-column channel, and group the remaining edge
detector so only the relevant colour group carries weights.  The final renderer
swaps its tiny role basis to `[edge, constant]`, improving `240/988 -> 240/960`
and score `17.8869 -> 17.9099`.  This remains a risky generator shortcut
(`93/100` extras), so only reuse the bias-constant role deletion when the
constant lane is genuinely redundant or after an explicit probe.

## `log-quantized-bbox-direct-einsum` (decode bbox starts with Log+QuantizeLinear, then render directly)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The task needs one or two bounding-box start coordinates,
and the previous graph uses `ArgMax`, prefix masks, or multiple crop
intermediates before rendering.  If a priority product or weighted moment gives
a monotone scalar for the coordinate, `Log` followed by a tuned
`QuantizeLinear` can turn that scalar into a small integer index.

**Recipe.** Build row and/or column priority scores with compact `Einsum`s,
take `Log`, quantize with a fitted scale/zero-point so legal coordinates map
to exact integer bins, and `Gather` the corresponding coordinate/basis row for
the final renderer:

```python
Einsum(input, priority_factors) -> row_score
Log(row_score) -> row_log
QuantizeLinear(row_log, scale, zero_point) -> row_idx_u8
Cast(row_idx_u8, INT32) -> row_idx
Gather(coord_basis, row_idx) -> row_basis
Einsum(input, row_basis, col_basis, ...) -> output
```

**Why.** It keeps bbox discovery scalar-sized and avoids materializing a full
per-coordinate mask.  The expensive crop/paint part can then be folded into
the final output contraction.

**Limits.** This is a finite-domain numeric decoder.  Check zero margins,
round-to-nearest boundaries, and every legal box coordinate.  If generated
extras expose coordinates near a quantization boundary, preserve a safer
fallback or probe the candidate.

**Tasks.** task031's 2026-06-30 team retune uses two
`Einsum -> Log -> QuantizeLinear -> Cast -> Gather` coordinate decoders for
the row and column starts, then one final direct renderer.  It reduces cost
`403 -> 231`, score `18.9994 -> 19.5559`.
task138's 2026-07-01 promoted port uses the same scalar-bound decoding shape
for row/column frame bounds: `Einsum` builds priority/mass sums, `Log` and
axis-aware `QuantizeLinear` recover packed bounds, and fp16 line factors feed
the final renderer.  The retune improves cost `2612 -> 2568`, score
`17.1321 -> 17.1491`.
task031 updated_v3 is a saved slow variant of the same direct-crop family:
it folds a two-entry root-sign vector into `P2`, replaces the score-selector
lane with a tiny epsilon in `Q2`, and reuses shared positive/negative root
factors to cover extra bbox tail aliases.  Local cost would drop `231 -> 177`,
but arc-gen[0] smoke estimates about `293s` required runtime, so it is stored
under `src/research/variants/` for probe rather than promoted.
task031 updated_v4 scales the foreground selector
so `Cast(Log(score), INT32)` lands on a small set of negative/zero indices,
then `Gather` scratch rows from otherwise-unused `P2` coordinate rows instead
of using `QuantizeLinear`.  This deletes the quantized-start tensors and
`q_scale`, reducing local cost `177 -> 174` versus v3 (`231 -> 174` versus
production).  Smoke estimates about `261s` required runtime, but a 2026-07-02
unconfirmed batch excluding hidden-rejected task109 matched Kaggle, confirming
this slow scratch-gather decoder as Kaggle-safe.
task031 updated_v6 is an even riskier scratch-row fold: repurpose the decoder
row `P2[29]`, which required/promotion footprints did not reach, to store
`M * [1, 1/2]` and replace explicit `RootNeg=[1,1/2]` operands by summed
references to `P2`.  This drops local cost `174 -> 172`, but it knowingly
risks rare `Cast(Log(score)) == -1` start-2 axes and smoke estimates about
`1007s` required runtime, so it is saved only as a slow/risky probe variant.

## `mode-gated-direct-output-einsum` (recover a tiny global mode and feed it into one final direct renderer)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The task has a few discrete global cases, such as legal
input sizes, panel layouts, or palette modes, and an otherwise direct-output
renderer becomes expensive only because it carries separate branch/crop
pipelines for those cases.

**Recipe.** Decode the global case into a tiny one-hot or short mode vector,
preferably from a scalar moment such as total mass, active-cell count, or a
small color count.  Feed that mode vector as one more operand of the final
high-arity output `Einsum`, and fold all branch-specific renderers into one
shared factorization.  The mode tensor should stay scalar/short-vector sized;
do not broadcast it to canvas size before the final renderer.

**Why.** A small counted mode vector can replace several full-canvas masks,
dynamic slices, or branch-specific coefficient banks.  It also lets the final
Einsum share row/column/color factors between modes, so the params term is
often lower than a literal table-per-case port.

**Limits.** The mode decoder must cover every legal generator case.  If the
mode comes from a lossy scalar such as total mass, check that no hidden legal
case aliases onto the wrong branch.  The final renderer is still a fitted
separator unless the mode/factorization is derived from the generator.

**Tasks.** task183 HF leaderboard port decodes the square size by
`mass = Einsum(input)` followed by `Equal(mass, [36,64,100])`, then passes the
3-lane `size_mode` directly into one `m2gram_p167` output `Einsum`.  This
replaces the previous memory-heavy size/crop route, improving cost
`442 -> 186` and score `18.9087 -> 19.7743`.

---

## `projective-ratio-winner-pad` (dynamic-scale QuantizeLinear ratio, ReduceMax winner, ConvInteger output pad)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The desired output is a single winning color/case chosen by
a ratio of high-order counts or moments, and the rest of the output is just a
padded one-cell or compact winner indicator.  A naive graph materializes
several decoded widths/heights/areas, compares candidates with boolean masks,
then pads the winner.

**Recipe.** Compute a numerator tensor and a matching denominator/scale tensor
with direct `Einsum` moments.  Use `QuantizeLinear(num, den, axis=...)` as the
finite-domain rounded ratio decoder.  Select the winner with `ReduceMax`,
derive a strict dynamic threshold such as `best - 1`, and use a tiny
`ConvInteger` with spatial pads as the graph output so only the winner remains
positive under `output > 0`.

**Why.** Dynamic-scale `QuantizeLinear` can replace explicit `Div/Floor/Cast`
or per-candidate quotient tables, while `ConvInteger` does the final threshold
and 30x30 padding in one counted output op.  The best cases store only the
small projective embeddings and a scalar cap input.

**Limits.** This is margin-sensitive.  Rounding boundaries, sparse-marker
holes, and hidden low-count cases can break the winner even when local extras
look good.  Keep the denominator nonzero on the legal domain and probe any
ratio retune that changes candidate ordering or cap logic.

**Tasks.** task355 `projective_micro` computes high-order numerator and
denominator tensors, applies `QuantizeLinear(num, den)` to get `score_u8`,
then uses `ReduceMax`, `best-1`, and a padded `ConvInteger` output.  The
Kaggle-confirmed HF port improves the previous production cost `216 -> 118`
and score `19.6247 -> 20.2293`.  Earlier rejected task355 probes show the
caveat: smaller ratio decoders with slightly different cap behavior passed
local promotion extras but scored 0.00 on Kaggle.
The 2026-06-28 batch tightens the same graph with
§`shrink-strict-winner-convinteger`: `Shrink(best,bias=1)` produces the
strict dynamic zero point directly, improving cost `118 -> 117`.

## `q-e-spatial-channel-einsum-collapse` (replace p70 C/z split-grid Einsum with length-30 q + 10x2 E)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A fixed small two-half bitmap task already has a memory-zero
graph-output `Einsum` using a 30x2 coordinate table `C` and a 10-value channel
tail `z`, usually cost `70`.  The output is a 4x4 or similarly tiny split-grid
boolean relation such as AND/OR between the two source halves.

**Recipe.** Replace `C` with one length-30 spatial lane vector `q`, and replace
the channel tail with one shared `E[10,2]` embedding.  Reuse `q` several times
inside the final `Einsum` so legal half coordinates produce stable signed
logits while inactive separator/tail lanes are zero or underflow away.  Reuse
`E` for both source-channel predicates and output-channel logits.  Keep the
graph output as signed fp32 logits and verify with ONNX Runtime because the
margins depend on fp32 product order.

**Why.** The old p70 form stores `C[30,2]` plus `z[10]`; the q/E form stores
`q[30]` plus `E[10,2]`, reducing params `70 -> 50` without adding intermediates.
This is a smaller, more structured instance of repeated-basis/subnormal
direct-output `Einsum`: the spatial vector handles half selection and padding,
while the channel embedding absorbs both input-color and output-color roles.

**Limits.** This is not a direct drop-in for every p70 split-grid solver.  The
spatial/color constants have to be refit for the exact boolean relation,
separator layout, active colors, and output color.  Treat newly fitted variants
as local gains until they pass required splits plus promotion extras or Kaggle
confirmation.

**Tasks.** task318 HF/local port applies this to the 4x4 top/bottom OR rule,
reducing cost `70 -> 50`, score `20.7515 -> 21.0880`, with required splits
and 100/100 generated extras passing locally.  task227 uses the same q/E
structure for the sibling 4x4 top/bottom AND rule, with the same cost and
score improvement.  Related p70 tasks task026, task144, and task236 still use
the older C/z form; they are candidates for an offline q/E refit, but the
downloaded leaderboard archive did not contain lower-cost q/E versions.
task144's later p40 retune removes `E[10,2]` as well: one fitted channel vector
`v[10]`, referenced six times with distinct Einsum labels, synthesizes the
source-color predicates and output logits through repeated products. The
spatial `q[30]` vector is likewise reused thirteen times. This keeps memory at
zero, reduces params/cost `50 -> 40`, and improves score
`21.0880 -> 21.3111`; all 30 known cases pass and HF confirms the exact graph.
For sibling q/E tasks, search a single-vector high-order channel embedding
before assuming the two-column channel basis is irreducible.

## `subnormal-coordinate-basis-collapse` (reuse tiny coordinate/channel bases so unwanted products underflow away)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct-output `Einsum` needs several related
row/column/channel predicates, but exact one-hot or parity tables dominate the
params term.  The legal domain has enough repeated products that a tiny basis
can be used many times inside the same contraction.

**Recipe.** Store one or two compact embeddings and reuse them repeatedly for
input channels, output channels, rows, columns, and local state predicates.
Choose some lanes near the fp32 subnormal range, or at small normal magnitudes
that become subnormal after repeated multiplication, so invalid aliases
underflow to zero while legal logits remain strictly positive.  Keep the graph
output as signed logits and verify on the target ORT version.

**Why.** The scorer counts an initializer once even if an `Einsum` references
it many times.  Reusing a tiny basis can delete whole parity vectors, channel
sign vectors, and local selector tables from already memory-zero graphs.

**Limits.** This is ORT fp32 contraction behavior, not symbolic algebra.
Operand order, dtype, and optimizer settings can affect margins.  Treat new
uses as aggressive unless required splits plus extras or Kaggle confirmation
show the underflow regime is stable.

**Tasks.** task252 HF port stores only `E[10,2]` plus a 30-value `Q` whose
alternate entries are around `1.345e-43`; one output `Einsum` reuses `E`
across many semantic roles and reaches cost `50` at memory zero, improving
from the prior cost about `96`.  task332 uses the same idea with one small
color embedding and a repeated column vector, improving cost `80 -> 50`.
task176 folds row-sum/state gain into `U`, `T`, and a subnormal-scale `Q`,
improving cost `80 -> 54`.
task231 updated_v2 applies the same principle to a periodic-continuation
direct renderer: the old `ReduceSum + Exp + Einsum` metric tail is replaced by
repeating one rank-2 row/column basis many times inside a single cubic
dot-power `Einsum`, while tiny subnormal tail rows suppress off-domain aliases.
This deletes the last 8 bytes of activation memory and reduces cost
`70 -> 60` with required splits and 100/100 extras passing locally.

## `root-orbit-projective-selector` (replace exact local selector ranks with root/orbit factored relations)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output projective selector uses many exact local
rank modes to distinguish positions, colors, or finite cyclic states.  A
smaller root/Fourier/orbit basis can separate only the reachable generator
relations, making exact identity reconstruction unnecessary.

**Recipe.** Slice the active compact input region, project it through cyclic
or root features, and reuse small orbit transition matrices repeatedly inside
one final `Einsum`.  Keep a low-dimensional core tensor for the actual
relation, while repeated root/orbit factors carry long-range equality,
adjacency, or phase constraints.

**Why.** Exact selector rank is often overkill for ARC generator families.
Root/orbit factors preserve the relations that matter while deleting many
local identity modes.  This can be a safer successor to hand-pruning selector
modes because the reduced basis still has an interpretable cyclic/orbit
structure.

**Limits.** Check for symmetry aliases: if two legal states share all chosen
root/orbit moments, no downstream core can recover the difference.  Add one
more orbit lane instead of relying on accidental sample coverage.

**Tasks.** task277 HF leaderboard port replaces the previous rank-pruned
local/global selector with a `root_orbit` direct renderer over a 10x10 cyan
slice.  It uses repeated `adj`, `Fin/Fout`, `root_ref`, and `orbit` factors
plus a tiny `core`, improving the previously confirmed cost `912 -> 674` and
score `18.1844 -> 18.4868`.

---

## `small-selector-linear-dependence-factorization` (replace one small selector table with an existing selector and a tiny transform)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output `Einsum` stores two small selector tables
with the same row/domain axis, and one table is exactly in the column span of
the other under fp32 precision.  This is most attractive when the base selector
is already needed elsewhere and the transform has fewer elements than the
deleted table.

**Recipe.** Solve `L1 == L0 @ M` for a tiny matrix `M`.  Replace each `L1`
operand in the final `Einsum` with `L0, M` and add the corresponding summed
latent label.  Verify the rebuilt ONNX, because the extra operand can perturb
floating-point accumulation even though the algebra is exact.

**Why.** The scorer counts initializer elements, not operator count.  Reusing
an existing selector and adding a smaller transform can reduce params without
creating any counted intermediate when the output is still one direct `Einsum`.

**Tasks.** task242 updated_v3 replaces a dedicated `L1[3,2]`
output-coordinate selector with `L0[3,2] @ M[2,2]`, saving two params at
unchanged 72-byte memory.  Required splits and 100/100 promotion extras pass.
task029 updated_v5 applies the same idea to a selector-only frame-colour
basis: the six-entry `Esel[2,3]` table is synthesized as
`Msel[2,2] @ U[2,30] @ C6[3,30]` inside the `sel_score` `Einsum`.  `U` and
`C6` are already counted by the renderer, so only four new `Msel` parameters
replace six deleted `Esel` parameters.  Cost drops `474 -> 472`, score
`18.8388 -> 18.8430`, with required splits and 100/100 extras passing.
task368 updated_v2 is the shared-latent variant: `ZStart[2,10]` is exactly an
affine transform of the already-needed `TMask[2,10]`, so four `ZStart`
occurrences in the direct renderer become `A[2,2] * TMask[2,10]` operands.
The same new latent label is deliberately shared across all four occurrences;
that is only valid because cross-role states are unreachable for the generator.
This deletes 20 params and adds 4, dropping cost `540 -> 524`, score
`18.7084 -> 18.7385`, with required splits and 100/100 extras passing.

## `einsum-diagonal-matrix-to-vector` (tie aligned latent labels and replace a fitted matrix with its diagonal vector)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A fitted feature path ends with
`source[c] * code[c,t] * A[t,s]`, but reachable states only need aligned
latent modes. The dense `A[d,d]` is diagonal, numerically near-diagonal, or can
be refit under the constraint `t == s` without changing verifier margins.

**Recipe.** Tie the two Einsum labels and replace the matrix operand by a
vector: `c,cT,TS -> S` becomes `c,cS,S -> S`. Refit the `d` vector values on
the finite corpus, then verify fp32 signs because deleting small off-diagonal
terms is not automatically algebraically exact.

**Why.** A `d*d` initializer becomes `d` parameters, saving `d*(d-1)` while
the feature remains the same tiny graph output/intermediate. This is the
diagonal specialization of small-selector factorization and is especially
cheap in an existing high-arity Einsum.

**Limits.** Do not apply when cross-mode coupling is semantically required or
when off-diagonal terms carry a narrow classification margin. Treat a refitted
version as finite-domain until the tied-mode invariant is proved.

**Tasks.** task222 updated_v1 changes the first colour-code feature from
`Mask[c], Hc[c,T], A[T,S]` with `A[3,3]` to
`Mask[c], Hc[c,S], Avec[S]`. The feature memory stays 12 bytes while params
fall `162 -> 156`; cost drops `174 -> 168` and score improves
`19.8409 -> 19.8760`. It passes 29/29 train/test/hidden cases and HF accepted
score 19.876036.
task222 updated_v2 keeps the diagonal feature but replaces the ten-entry
`Mask[10]` factor with a three-entry `Qmask[3]`, reusing `Hc` and `Qmask`
directly in the first Einsum. Memory remains 12 bytes while params drop
`156 -> 149`, cost `168 -> 161`, and the exact graph passes 29/29 cases with
HF-confirmed score `19.8760 -> 19.9186`.
task222 updated_v3 removes the remaining three-entry `Avec` factor by reusing
the existing `Hc`/`Qmask` operands directly in the first feature Einsum.  The
feature memory stays 12 bytes while params drop `149 -> 146`, cost `161 ->
158`, and score improves `19.9186 -> 19.9374`; all 29 required cases pass and
HF confirms the graph.

## `common-nan-tail-absorption` (fold output-tail suppression into shared coordinate factors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output `Einsum` uses valid coordinate factors plus
an extra mask or bias only to suppress rows/columns outside the active
generator canvas.  The invalid tail coordinates are never supposed to produce
positive logits.

**Recipe.** Put `NaN` lanes directly into the shared coordinate basis for
tail positions, and reuse that basis throughout the direct renderer.  Under
the verifier/Kaggle `output > 0` threshold, tail logits involving those lanes
compare false, so a separate tail mask or output bias can disappear.

**Why.** This extends the confirmed ConvTranspose NaN-tail trick to
memory-zero or near-memory-zero direct `Einsum` graphs: the NaN lane is not an
internal branch decision, it is part of the graph output logit construction.

**Limits.** Use only when NaN-tainted cells/channels are guaranteed to be
false outputs.  Do not feed NaN-bearing tensors into internal comparisons,
quantizers, or integer casts.  Probe if a new graph relies on NaN propagation
through anything other than the final signed-logit output.

**Tasks.** task376 `direct_p122_absorb_common_nan_tail` uses a shared
coordinate basis `P` whose rows 21..29 are `[NaN, NaN]`, deleting separate
tail suppression while keeping memory zero.  The HF port improves cost
`158 -> 122` and score `19.9374 -> 20.1960`.
task376 `rect32_p114` keeps the same NaN-padded `P` tail but refits the
direct-output relation from the older cubic `U/D/V` factorization into one
rectangular core `T` plus compact `Dz`/`Dy` factors.  The graph remains a
single memory-zero `Einsum`, and params drop `118 -> 114` with HF confirmation
at score `20.2638`.  This is a useful final-pass check for memory-zero
direct renderers: once NaN tail masking is safe, refit the active relation
core under the already-shared coordinate basis instead of preserving an older
symbolic polynomial decomposition.

---

## `shared-stencil-convtranspose-conv-render` (reuse one signed kernel for detection and rendering)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A small fixed stencil both detects the relevant phase/offset
and renders the output.  A naive graph stores one kernel for a detector and a
second related kernel for the renderer, or materializes a detector score map
then performs a separate table lookup.

**Recipe.** Store one signed stencil `W` and reuse it in both directions:
`ConvTranspose(input, W, bias) -> score`, then `Conv(score, W) -> output`.
Retune the optional bias so the first op emits only the small state/phase map
needed by the second op.  Because `W` is one initializer referenced twice, the
params term counts it once.

**Why.** The graph pays a small memory term for the intermediate score map but
deletes a second kernel/table.  This is especially useful when the detector
map is tiny, such as 3x3 or 4x3, and the same spatial pattern is naturally the
transpose of the renderer.

**Limits.** This is different from arbitrary dynamic Conv weights: both Conv
weights are static initializers, and only the data flow changes direction.
Check signed margins carefully because one kernel must satisfy both roles.
Very large fp32 coefficients can be useful here to create overflow-separated
logits, but keep them inside this static-weight reuse pattern; do not treat
them as a general NaN/overflow classifier trick.

**Tasks.** task395 and task386 team ports use exactly
`ConvTranspose -> Conv` with shared `W`.  task395 improves
`mem/params 36/30 -> 36/20`, and task386 improves `48/30 -> 48/20`, both
Kaggle-confirmed in the 2026-06-24 team batch.
The 2026-07-06 HF leaderboard retune for task395 drops the shared kernel
further to `memory/params 36/11` (`cost 47`, score `21.1499`), showing that
once the shared-W topology is fixed, the remaining win is often pruning
inactive output/filter channels rather than changing ops.

---

## `scalar-ratio-state-direct-einsum` (recover one runtime ratio then render with a direct-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The rule depends on a one-dimensional continuous or rational
state that can be recovered from a few global moments, and the rest of the
solution is a finite renderer conditioned on that state.  A multi-step graph
often builds classifier planes, masks, or QLinear tails just to carry that
state to the output.

**Recipe.** Compute two or three scalar moments with small `Einsum` reductions,
form the ratio or normalized scalar with `Div`, concatenate `[1, p]` or a
short polynomial basis, and feed it into one final output `Einsum` with static
coordinate/channel factors.  Keep the ratio tensor tiny; do not broadcast it
to a full canvas before the final contraction.

**Why.** The ratio can replace wide classifier grids and case tables while
preserving an algorithmic interpretation.  The direct output contraction is
the only place where the scalar expands to `(1,10,30,30)`.

**Limits.** The denominator must be nonzero on the official domain, and the
ratio margins must remain stable under fp32 ORT arithmetic.  If the generator
has rare degenerate states, keep a fallback branch or probe before promotion.

**Tasks.** task165 team port computes two tiny descriptors for row/column
state, sums them into a 2-lane vector, and renders directly with one final
`Einsum`.  The 2026-06-24 confirmed version first retuned the state and
channel factors to memory/params `24/116`, replacing the previous
memory-heavy classifier path while keeping only `rowD`, `colD`, and `P` as
counted intermediates.  The later HF leaderboard retune folds out one tiny
state reducer and keeps the same scalar-ratio interpretation with two
`Einsum` ops, reaching `8/104`, cost `140 -> 112`, and score
`20.0584 -> 20.2815`.

---

## `tiny-slice-state-direct-renderer` (read only tiny dynamic windows then render with one direct-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task needs a runtime source/target relationship, but the
relationship is fully determined by a few small windows around detected
coordinates.  The expensive version carries full-canvas crops, masks, or
path-finding intermediates.

**Recipe.** Use scalar moment/cast arithmetic to compute dynamic `Slice`
starts for only the tiny state windows, such as a 2-cell target probe and a
5x2 source strip.  Feed those tiny tensors directly into a large final
`Einsum` that encodes the finite path/edge relation and emits logits.  Keep
the sliced tensors compact and avoid padding them back to canvas size before
the final output op.

**Why.** Dynamic `Slice` is acceptable when shape inference still knows the
fixed output size.  Replacing full-canvas state with tiny windows can shrink
memory by thousands even if the final fitted renderer has more params.

**Limits.** Dynamic slice coordinates must be statically shaped and within the
valid generator domain.  This pattern is not a reason to use dynamic-shape
`Slice`/`Pad`; only the start values should be runtime-derived.

**Tasks.** task182 team port slices `target23_f` `(1,2,1,1)` and `src_small`
`(1,1,5,2)`, then uses a direct pathword `Einsum` to render the answer.  It
replaces a large Conv/Equal/QLinear staging graph, improving
`mem/params 3183/281 -> 148/636` (+1.4858 score) while passing the promoted
team batch.

---

## `row-bitset-split-prefix-render` (pack rows to integer bitsets, split columns, and render with unrolled bitwise prefixes)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The rule is row-local or column-local and can be expressed
as intervals, parity, or reachability along rows.  A naive solution stores
per-cell prefix masks, repeated MaxPools, or dense row/column relation planes.

**Recipe.** Pack each row or column into an integer bitset with an `Einsum`
using powers of two.  Split the packed integer into scalar column bits with
`BitwiseAnd`/thresholds, perform the needed scan with unrolled `BitwiseXor`,
`BitwiseOr`, `BitwiseAnd`, `BitwiseNot`, or shifts, then compose the output
from the resulting scalar masks.  If the legal grid size varies among a few
values, use small `Where` guards to select the valid row mask instead of
building separate full-canvas masks.

**Why.** A 30-cell row can often be represented by one scalar instead of 30
cells of intermediate memory.  Bitwise ops on packed scalars are cheap under
the scorer and can replace entire prefix/suffix tensor families.

**Limits.** Keep packed values within the dtype range used by ORT.  For 30-bit
rows use int32/uint32-style operations deliberately and verify exact behavior
under the target opset.  This is best when the output can be reconstructed
from row bitsets without unpacking multiple full intermediate planes.

**Tasks.** task338 team port packs colored rows, splits the resulting column
bits, performs unrolled bitwise prefix/parity logic, and size-gates the valid
row mask for generator sizes 10/15/20/25.  The confirmed promotion reduced
cost from the previous production graph to `mem/params 1611/345`, improving
score by about +0.51 in the team batch.

task204 updated_v17 uses the same scalar-bitset idea transposed by axis: it
packs black/blue rows 0..19 into one `uint32` per column, derives vertical
edge toggles as `blue & (blue << 1)`, runs forward/reverse scalar parity scans
across the 20 legal columns, and renders red/orange/black by bit-testing
against row powers in the final output.  This replaces 20x20 nearest-edge
MaxPool planes and a QLinear tail with smaller bitwise scalar state, improving
local `mem/params 6340/104 -> 3032/132` and score `16.2291 -> 16.9404` with
required splits and 100/100 extras passing.
The 2026-06-28 team batch confirms the same family on larger production
ports: task023 uses 26 MaxPool probes plus `BitwiseAnd/Or/Not` composition and
QLinearConv tails, improving cost `1484 -> 1407`; task367 packs black/gray
row bitsets with two `Einsum`s and a long scalar bitwise scan, improving cost
`4308 -> 4241`.  The 2026-07-01 task367 retune keeps the same bitset scan but
removes a few redundant `BitShift`/`BitwiseAnd`/`BitwiseNot` intermediates and
shrinks counted memory `3860 -> 3820` at unchanged params, improving score
`16.6493 -> 16.6588`.

**Complement-derived support variant.** If one foreground colour marks every
border cell and the active square is fully occupied by either border or
background, avoid packing the background/black channel separately.  Pack the
foreground column bitset, derive the active square rowmask once from the
one-hot input (`sqrt(sum input[c,r,w] * 2^r * 2^w)` on square grids), and
recover background column bits as `rowmask XOR foreground_bits` with small
size guards for columns outside the active width.  task204 updated_v28 deletes
the full black-channel pack and a fill-vector staging tensor this way,
improving local cost `2898 -> 2764` and score `17.0282 -> 17.0756` while
passing required splits and the 98/100 promotion gate.

## `centered-segment-feature-retune` (replace absolute finite geometry features with centered int8 segment features)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A small final classifier consumes endpoint/segment
features such as `[const, lo + hi, lo * hi, fixed, fixed^2]`, and the legal
coordinates live in a compact integer range.

**Recipe.** Center each coordinate around a shared midpoint with int8
`Cast/Sub`, build the same polynomial feature bank in the centered domain,
and retune the downstream linear or QLinear classifier coefficients for the
centered basis.  Reuse one centered constant row when possible.

**Why.** Centered values keep intermediate dtypes small, share coordinate
preprocessing across several candidate segments, and can delete wider
absolute-coordinate feature tensors without changing the finite-domain sign
separation.

**Limits.** This is an algebraic retune, not just a dtype cast.  Recompute the
classifier coefficients and verify margins on required plus extras.

**Tasks.** task066 updated_v6 replaces the v5 absolute uint16 segment feature
path with shared int8 centered segment features and a const=9 row, improving
cost `711 -> 593` and score `18.4333 -> 18.6148`.

---

## `route-folded-target-color-state` (derive target colour from an existing route tensor)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A graph carries a routed branch/state tensor whose
nonzero channels already identify the eventual target colours, while a
separate dynamic Slice or small color probe exists only to recover that same
target colour.

**Recipe.** Multiply or gate the route tensor by the existing branch/color
flags to remove contamination channels, then reduce the remaining route
counts into the target-colour vector.  Feed that vector directly to the final
renderer and delete the dynamic target-color Slice/probe.

**Why.** The route tensor has already paid for the finite branch selection.
Using it as the target-colour carrier removes a tiny dynamic window and its
staging memory while keeping the same renderer semantics.

**Limits.** The route tensor must have exact support on the official
generator domain.  If extra route channels can be nonzero, keep the explicit
probe or add a guard.

**Tasks.** task182 updated_v3 derives the `[2,3]` target-colour count from
`RouteOut * Chan * (1 - colour1_flag)`, deleting the target-centre Slice and
improving cost `758 -> 720`, score `18.3693 -> 18.4207`.

---

## `single-step-quantized-width-decode` (decode a bounded integer width directly with QuantizeLinear)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A bounded integer parameter is currently decoded by an
intermediate scalar plus a small linear table, but the parameter is already a
monotone function of a runtime moment on the legal domain.

**Recipe.** Choose a `QuantizeLinear` scale so `round(moment / scale)` equals
the desired integer for every generator-valid case.  Feed the quantized byte
directly to the downstream renderer or kernel selector and delete the
intermediate moment-to-width table.

**Why.** `QuantizeLinear` can perform a finite-domain affine decoder in one
op with a scalar scale.  It often removes a small `QLinearMatMul` plus a
temporary width/prow tensor.

**Limits.** Check all legal finite cases for rounding boundaries, not only
samples.  Avoid scales where fp32 round-to-nearest can hit a half-integer
margin.

**Tasks.** task208 updated_v11 decodes the hole width directly from the row
pair moment `P` using scale 22, removing `prow_u8` and the scalar width
decoder.  Cost improves `2629 -> 2627`.

---

## `rank-pruned-projective-selector` (drop exact selector modes when sign separation remains stable)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A direct-output projective renderer uses an exact
rank-N selector basis to represent identity/local and all-ones/global modes,
but the task only needs sign-correct separation over the generator domain.

**Recipe.** Keep the all-ones/global mode exactly, drop low-value zero-sum
modes from the local selector, and retune the final penalty/bias so all
required and diagnostic cases keep positive true logits and non-positive
wrong logits.  Promote only when the extras gate passes; otherwise preserve
as a probe variant.

**Why.** Exact Kronecker-delta reconstruction can be stronger than the task
requires.  A lower-rank projection can save initializer parameters while
still separating all reachable cases.

**Limits.** This is distribution-sensitive.  It is safe only when required
and extras cover the reachable generator family well, or after Kaggle probe.

**Tasks.** task277 updated_v14 drops two zero-sum modes from the exact
rank-10 local/global selector, retunes the global penalty, and passes
100/100 promotion extras.  Cost improves `996 -> 912`, score
`18.0963 -> 18.1844`.  The later Kaggle-confirmed
§`root-orbit-projective-selector` version supersedes this particular task277
variant with cost `674`, but the rank-pruning idea remains useful for
local-only probes when no root/orbit factorization is known.

---

## `leaderboard-single-einsum-projective-renderer` (collapse a whole solver into one graph-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The task has a small finite set of geometric/object
parameters and the existing graph first decodes those parameters into
intermediate masks before rendering the final grid.

**Recipe.** Fit or hand-factor the renderer as a direct multilinear map from
the one-hot input and compact coordinate/color bases to the output logits.
Use the final `Einsum` output directly as graph output so the large rendered
canvas is not counted as an intermediate.  Prefer tiny signed/projective
bases over exact one-hot coordinate tables when sign separation is enough.

**Why.** For small ARC families the solver and renderer are often both finite
rank.  A single graph-output `Einsum` can trade a few initializer parameters
for zero counted memory and delete all staging tensors.

**Limits.** This is only safe when the fitted factors separate every legal
case with margin.  Inspect zero margins, because the verifier uses
`output > 0` and exact zero is false.  Large fitted factors can become slow;
smoke-test representative arc-gen samples before promoting.

**Tasks.** The confirmed leaderboard batch used this pattern heavily.
task175 improved cost `282 -> 46`, score `19.3581 -> 21.1714`; task273
improved `460 -> 104`, score `18.8688 -> 20.3556`; task251 improved
`1584 -> 426`, score `17.6323 -> 18.9456`.
task273 R3 further factors the 16-element shared `U[2,2,2,2]` renderer core
into two independently summed rank-2 projective sides plus a 2-lane sign vector,
dropping cost `104 -> 102` while preserving the same zero-memory direct-output
Einsum pattern.

---

## `trig-projective-coordinate-renderer` (use low-rank sinusoidal/projective coordinate bases)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct renderer needs distinguishable row/column
locations, offsets, or orientations, but exact 30-wide coordinate identity
tables dominate params or memory.

**Recipe.** Replace exact coordinate selectors with a small projective basis,
often two columns using smooth/trigonometric functions or affine/projective
coordinates.  Retune the final renderer so the legal coordinates are
sign-separated rather than exactly reconstructed.

**Why.** Many generators only require selecting among a constrained set of
positions or orientations.  Low-rank coordinate embeddings can keep enough
separation for the final logits while deleting exact 30x30 selector tensors.

**Limits.** This is a fitted finite-domain technique.  It must be checked on
the generator-valid coordinate range, and it is risky for tasks where hidden
cases can place objects outside the trained coordinate manifold.

**Tasks.** task345 uses a two-column coordinate basis and one direct output
`Einsum`, improving cost `481 -> 80`, memory `290 -> 0`, and score
`18.8241 -> 20.6180`.

## `cp-tucker-output-collapse` (replace candidate enumeration with a fitted tensor factorization)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The old solution enumerates many candidate placements,
objects, or local relations, then reduces them with `Max`/`Min`/winner logic.
The task family is finite enough that the final output tensor has low
effective rank.

**Recipe.** Factor the candidate-to-output map into compact row/column/color
and relation bases, then emit a single graph-output `Einsum` or a tiny stack
of `Einsum`s.  Keep only the final factorized logits; delete the candidate
volume.

**Why.** Candidate enumeration is memory-expensive under the sum-of-internals
model.  A fitted CP/Tucker-style factorization can eliminate thousands of
counted memory cells even if it increases initializer params.

**Limits.** Params can rise, so use this only when the deleted memory is much
larger than the added factors.  Verify margins on generator-valid extras or
Kaggle-probe if the factorization is aggressive.

**Tasks.** task349 collapses a high-memory composition/search graph into a
single fitted factorized renderer, improving cost `11667 -> 2301`, memory
`10740 -> 0`, and score `15.6355 -> 17.2589`.
task066 updated_v15 applies the same low-rank factorization idea to a dense
finite classifier core: the `KPAIR[5,3,3]` initializer is replaced by
`KA[5,4]`, `KB[3,4]`, and `KC[3,4]` factors inside the direct `Einsum`, while
the existing random case decoder is retained.  A scalar mode initializer is
also absorbed into the random branch.  Params fall `173 -> 171`, memory
`129` is unchanged, cost `302 -> 300`, and score improves `19.2896 -> 19.2962`
with 30/30 required cases and HF confirmation.

---

## `lppool-negative-stride-zero-param-remap` (use LpPool negative pads/strides for fixed crop/remap)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The required transform is a fixed crop, reversal, or
rotation-like remap and no learned constants are truly needed.

**Recipe.** Use `LpPool` with `kernel_shape=[1,1]`, negative pads, and
negative strides to express the fixed spatial remap directly from the input
to output.  Because there are no initializers and the pool output is the graph
output, the model can score as zero cost.

**Why.** A degenerate pool can act as an address remapper.  It can replace
small RoiAlign/Gather/selector tables with no params and no counted
intermediates.

**Limits.** Negative pads/strides are implementation-sensitive.  This pattern
is Kaggle-confirmed for the exact task140 shape/remap, but should be
smoke-tested and probed before using on a new task.

**Tasks.** task140 uses one `LpPool` node with negative pads/strides and no
initializers, improving cost `5 -> 0` and score `23.3906 -> 25.0000`.

---

## `negative-stride-maxpool-remap` (use degenerate MaxPool to flip or crop runtime tensors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A larger solver has a small runtime tensor such as a
dynamic kernel, template, or transform matrix that must be flipped, cropped, or
strided before a later `QLinearConv`/`MatMulInteger`/stamping tail.  The naive
adapter uses `Slice`, `Gather`, `Expand`, or a small static index table.

**Recipe.** Use `MaxPool` with `kernel_shape=[1,1]` and carefully chosen
negative pads or negative strides to remap the runtime tensor.  For a pure
flip, use `strides=[-1,-1]` or a one-axis negative stride; for a crop, use
negative pads to discard border cells while keeping static output shape:

```python
MaxPool(W, kernel_shape=[1, 1], strides=[-1, -1],
        pads=[-top, -left, -bottom, -right]) -> W_flipped_or_cropped
```

Because the pooled window is one cell, `MaxPool` acts as an address remapper,
not as an aggregation.  Keep it on small tensors; if applied to a full canvas,
the counted memory can outweigh the saved params.

**Why.** Attribute-only remaps can delete index initializers and adapter
nodes.  This is the intermediate-tensor counterpart to
§`lppool-negative-stride-zero-param-remap`: it is not usually a whole solution,
but it cleans up runtime kernels inside already optimized graphs.

**Limits.** Negative strides/pads are implementation-sensitive.  Use only when
ONNX shape inference still proves static shapes and Kaggle/ORT confirmation is
available for the exact graph.  Do not rely on it to hide large intermediates;
it is a normal scored tensor remap.  A simultaneous cropped reverse is not
automatically safe even when shape inference succeeds: the task219
`3x10 -> 3x8` reverse-template trial with
`kernel_shape=[1,1]`, `strides=[-1,-1]`, and `pads=[-2,-9,-2,-7]` inferred the
desired shape but segfaulted ORT 1.24.4.  Keep negative-step `Slice` or use a
two-step remap unless the exact cropped-reverse `MaxPool` graph is verified.

**Tasks.** The 2026-07-01 leaderboard batch confirmed this as a cleanup
technique.  task101 replaces a `Slice + Expand` dynamic chain-kernel adapter
with two degenerate `MaxPool` remaps, reducing params `195 -> 182` inside the
same large runtime-kernel solver.  task158 replaces three fixed `Gather`
adapters over a transform matrix with `MaxPool` horizontal/vertical/both flips,
reducing params `149 -> 146`.  task170 similarly replaces two gather-style
geometry adapters with extra `MaxPool` remaps, improving cost `523 -> 521`.

---

## `ratio-quantizelinear-phase-decode` (decode finite geometry cases with moment ratios and QuantizeLinear)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A graph computes several shape moments or route counts,
then uses a large branch table to identify a small finite phase, period, or
case index.

**Recipe.** Build numerator and denominator moments with compact `Einsum`s.
Feed them to `Div` or directly to dynamic-scale `QuantizeLinear` to recover a
u8 phase/code.  Use that code as a `Gather`, `QLinearMatMul`, or compact final
renderer input instead of materializing all candidates.

**Why.** Finite case selection is often the real task.  Moment ratios plus
rounding can replace large masks and threshold cascades with a few scalar
features.

**Limits.** Rounding boundaries matter.  Check every legal finite case, not
only public samples, and avoid half-integer margins unless intentionally
using banker's rounding.

**Tasks.** task105 uses repeated ratio/`QuantizeLinear` phase decoding before
a compact renderer, improving cost `1051 -> 215`, score
`18.0425 -> 19.6294`.  task370 combines ratio decoding, small gathers, and a
`QLinearMatMul` case tail, improving cost `2058 -> 505`, score
`17.3705 -> 18.7754`.
The 2026-07-01 leaderboard batch confirmed smaller retunes in the same family:
task105's repeated projective ratio decoders and compact final renderer improve
from cost `180 -> 176`, score `19.8070 -> 19.8295`; task370's
ratio/case-tail port improves `492 -> 490`, score `18.8015 -> 18.8056`; and
task170 combines log/quantized geometry decoding with the
§`negative-stride-maxpool-remap` adapter to improve `523 -> 521`.
task370 updated_v3 then replaces the `bg_id * nonblack_count` staging path
with a direct colour-difference moment `Einsum(input,Hc,RU,color_diff2)`.
This keeps the same ratio/phase renderer but removes one counted scalar
intermediate, improving memory `202 -> 198` at unchanged params `288`;
required splits and `100/100` promotion extras pass locally.
task370 updated_v6 folds the background-minus-one colour selector into the
existing `RU`/`Mb`/`D` factors: the dynamic colour vector becomes `[bg, 1]`
instead of `[1-bg, 1]`, and the seed-minus-background scalar is recovered by
signing the same compact moment rather than materializing `one_minus_bg`.
Memory drops `198 -> 194` with params unchanged; required splits and
`100/100` promotion extras pass locally.

## `imagescaler-scalar-affine` (use ImageScaler as a tiny scalar affine transform)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A graph needs one or two scalar affine transforms, usually
for a Conv/ConvTranspose bias, and the equivalent initializer/vector path
would cost more.

**Recipe.** Feed the scalar into `ImageScaler` with the desired `scale` and
`bias` attributes, then route the result through `Where` or directly into the
consumer.  Keep the input/output shapes statically known.

**Why.** `ImageScaler` stores scale/bias as attributes rather than normal
initializers.  For tiny scalar affine tails this can reduce counted params by
one or two cells.

**Limits.** `ImageScaler` is experimental and the local scorer warns about
it.  It was accepted by Kaggle in the confirmed batch, but use it only for
small confirmed/probed savings and avoid depending on it for broad new
architectures.

**Tasks.** An earlier task288 variant used two scalar `ImageScaler` nodes to
produce a dynamic ConvTranspose bias branch, improving cost `159 -> 158`.
The current Kaggle-confirmed task288 production graph supersedes that path
with §`convtranspose-dynamic-bias-cascade`, reducing cost to `119` and using
no `ImageScaler` nodes.  Keep `ImageScaler` in mind for tiny scalar-affine
tails, but prefer the ConvTranspose cascade when the bias can be extracted
from the static input-as-weight tensor.

## `tfidfvectorizer-signature-lookup-extension` (decode a finite signature through TfIdfVectorizer)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The task can be reduced to a small integer signature and a
finite parameter/code lookup, but a normal one-hot or Gather table is too
expensive.

**Recipe.** Hash the relevant object moments into an int32 token sequence,
add static offsets or terminators, then use `TfIdfVectorizer` n-gram
attributes as the finite lookup.  Feed the decoded vector to the final
renderer.

**Why.** `TfIdfVectorizer` can encode sparse finite dictionaries in node
attributes and may beat explicit lookup tensors for small codebooks.

**Limits.** Token collisions must be impossible on the legal generator
domain.  Keep token sequences short and static; this is not a general text
processing trick.

Transfer boundary: task101 looked like a direct selected-row opportunity
because its final contraction consumes `case[9]`, `H[9,30]`, and `W[9,30]`.
However, `case` is a dense signed classifier vector rather than a one-hot
state.  Replacing `H/W` with ArgMax-selected two-token `TfIdfVectorizer`
row LUTs lowered the static cost estimate `801 -> 787` (`memory/params`
`232/569 -> 728/59`) but failed the first smoke output because ArgMax is not
equivalent to the original weighted contraction.  Do not apply selected-row
LUT compression to a continuous classifier state; first prove an exact
discrete signature or preserve the full factor tables.  The same caution
applies to task216's coordinate bases, which are also consumed both as
selected rows and as full tables.

**Tasks.** task013 extends the existing finite-signature lookup pattern:
`GatherND`/moment `Einsum` creates a signature, token offsets feed
`TfIdfVectorizer`, and a final `Einsum` renders the answer.  The 2026-06-28
batch confirms more lookup shapes: task021 uses quartic self-similarity
moments plus two `TfIdfVectorizer` nodes and a RoiAlign sampler; task066
packs row/line bitfields, decodes one selector with `TfIdfVectorizer`, and
then renders with bitwise arithmetic; task109 uses `ReduceL1`/QuantizeLinear
counts plus a tiny `TfIdfVectorizer` gate before a direct renderer; task119
and task183 use compact `Einsum` signatures feeding a single vectorizer.
The 2026-06-30 batch retuned two of these patterns.  task021 removed the
`Reciprocal/Add` normalization around the quartic signature while keeping two
`TfIdfVectorizer` nodes plus `RoiAlign`, reducing cost `64 -> 50`.
task109 replaced the quantized count-code branch with
`ThresholdedRelu(alpha=9.5)` plus a larger vectorizer token table, reducing
cost `381 -> 358`.
The 2026-07-01 task109 leaderboard port is a stronger count-signature form:
`ReduceL1(input) -> ReduceMax(counts) -> Cast(INT32) -> TfIdfVectorizer`
selects the finite mode from only the maximum colour count, while the final
high-arity `Einsum` still receives the full count vector repeatedly.  It
removes the `ThresholdedRelu` gate and improves the confirmed production graph
from cost `358 -> 319`, score `19.1195 -> 19.2348`.
task109 updated_v5 deletes the four-entry `K3` selector by retuning
unreachable `O[:,29,0]` tail entries so `sum_{E,F} O[H,E,F]` synthesizes
`[0,0,0,1]` inside the final contraction.  The scratch entries would otherwise
light row/column 29 too broadly, so the same direct-output `Einsum` multiplies
by a free `input[n,G,r,t]` occupancy mask.  Cost drops `319 -> 314` with
required splits plus `100/100` extras passing.
task392 updated_v3 folds the foreground colour into the finite moment hash
itself, then uses three `TfIdfVectorizer` decoders for start row, start column,
and colour.  The decoded colour is scattered into a tiny `ConvInteger` kernel,
deleting the previous `GlobalLpPool/Split` colour-presence path and reducing
cost `323 -> 296` with 100/100 promotion extras.
task066 updated_v18 shows the same family can sometimes be compressed by
packing paired discrete roles into fewer tokens before the vectorizer.  Its
selector key replaces a four-token finite signature with two modulo-256 tokens:
`left_endpoint * 20 + right_blocker` and `green_column * 20 + red_column`.
After projecting the old dispatch onto that packed domain, cost drops
`543 -> 411` while the promotion gate stays `100/100`.
task066 updated_v23 folds one more endpoint/gating branch into the existing
finite-signature decoder by deleting the `nonblack` vector plus one
`Einsum`/`Where` pair.  The exact ONNX was accepted by the HF leaderboard and
reduces production cost `336 -> 317`, score `19.1829 -> 19.2411`.
HF-confirmed task029/task090/task133 add stronger evidence that TfIdf can be
used as a compact dictionary even when the final renderer is not otherwise
tiny.  task090 gathers six discriminating input cells, feeds one 6-gram
`TfIdfVectorizer`, reduces the vectorizer output to packed case parameters,
and replaces the previous arithmetic case decoder, dropping cost
`1091 -> 438`.  task029 uses four vectorizers plus gathers to reduce cost
`466 -> 404`; task133 uses nine vectorizers inside a larger quantized renderer
for a small but confirmed `5210 -> 5209` trim.  Prefer this when the legal
domain has a handful of exact witness cells or moment hashes and a dense
`Gather` table would spend more counted memory than vectorizer attributes.
Do not generalize every leaderboard TfIdf candidate blindly: the same batch
proved task119's downloaded local-gain vectorizer variant was hidden-rejected
on Kaggle (`0.0`) and it was excluded from promotion.

## `regexfullmatch-signature-lut` (use RegexFullMatch attributes as finite signature dictionaries)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task can be reduced to a scalar or short vector signature
whose legal values form a finite set, and each output bit/lane is membership in
one subset of those values.  A dense lookup tensor or many `Gather` tables
would be counted, while regex patterns live in node attributes.

**Recipe.** Compute a stable numeric signature, cast it to string with
`Cast(to=STRING)`, then use one `RegexFullMatch` node per finite predicate.
Each regex is an anchored alternation of accepted signature strings.  Combine
the boolean predicate outputs with `Concat`, `Where`, `DepthToSpace`, or a
quantized renderer such as `ConvInteger`/`QLinearConv`.

**Why.** The dictionaries are serialized as operator attributes rather than
counted initializers.  This can be cheaper than an explicit case table when
there are many sparse membership predicates but the ONNX file still stays under
the submission cap.

**Tasks.** The 2026-07-10 HF leaderboard promotion made this a confirmed local
pattern.  task134 hashes the grid with one `Einsum`, casts the signature to a
string, decodes pattern bits with 18 `RegexFullMatch` nodes, uses
`DepthToSpace` to form the polarity tile, and feeds a tiny dynamic
`ConvInteger` tail; local cost improves `217 -> 79`.  task158 uses 227 regex
predicates as a large sparse boolean canvas decoder but still beats the
previous graph by replacing thousands of counted params (`4280 -> 1932`
cost).  task170 and task219 use smaller regex dictionaries before quantized or
MaxPool-renderer tails.

**Limits.** String formatting must match the target ONNX Runtime exactly.
Scientific notation, rounding, signed zeros, and cast dtype choices can change
the produced strings, so promote only graphs accepted by the target scorer or
with exact local verification under the same runtime.  Attribute tables are
uncounted by the memory/params scorer but still affect ONNX file size.

---

## `convtranspose-seed-prefix-renderer` (use ConvTranspose as a cheap seed/broadcast stage)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The solution needs to stamp or broadcast a small seed,
prefix, or object template before a final direct renderer, and the current
implementation stores a large expanded template.

**Recipe.** Use one or two `ConvTranspose` nodes to inflate compact seed
signals or prefixes into the needed spatial support, then combine them with a
small direct `Einsum` renderer.  Prefer input-as-weight or output-as-logits
variants when legal.

**Why.** `ConvTranspose` can express sparse expansion/stamping with a small
kernel while avoiding explicit full-canvas initializer tables.

**Limits.** Bias length must be legal and full-sized when bias is used.  Check
that the ConvTranspose output shape is statically inferable by ONNX shape
inference.

**Tasks.** task035 uses two `ConvTranspose` stages plus a compact renderer,
improving cost `646 -> 221`, score `18.5281 -> 19.6007`.

## `l2-moment-discriminator` (use ReduceL2 as a compact finite-case feature)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** Several candidate shapes or counts differ by a Euclidean
norm-like statistic, and the current graph builds a larger count vector or
case classifier.

**Recipe.** Use `ReduceL2` over the relevant support to produce a scalar or
small vector feature, optionally `Gather` or cast it into a compact basis,
then let the final renderer discriminate the finite cases.

**Why.** `ReduceL2` can combine count and magnitude information in one
operator.  For one-hot or sparse masks it often encodes enough of the finite
case while avoiding multiple `ReduceSum`/threshold branches.

**Limits.** Norm collisions are possible.  Confirm that every legal case has
a unique or separable value after fp32 rounding.

**Tasks.** task388 uses `ReduceL2` plus small gathers before the final
`Einsum`, improving cost `782 -> 227`, score `18.3381 -> 19.5751`.
task328's 2026-06-28 team port uses `ReduceL2` plus `Pow` and two compact
`Einsum`s as a finite-case moment discriminator, cutting cost
`3558 -> 640` and score `16.8230 -> 18.5385`.
task328's later binary-basis retune keeps the same `ReduceL2 -> Pow -> Einsum`
architecture but replaces `BASE[3,2] + OUTV[3,2,30] + MAP[2,2,3]` with
`BR[2,2,2] + V[2,2,30]`. Repeated use of the powered binary basis absorbs the
old three-state map; a follow-up reuses `PAIR` and diagonal/repeated `BR`
labels to remove the separate `FIX`, `WREL`, and `CS` vectors. Memory/params
change `28/304 -> 36/232`, total cost falls `332 -> 268`, and score improves
`19.1949 -> 19.4090`; all 30 known cases pass and HF confirms the exact graph.
When a moment renderer already uses `Pow`, search state-basis arity, repeated
operand factorization, and tiny correction-vector elimination together rather
than only reducing the final coordinate rank.

---

## `reciprocal-normalized-direct-einsum` (divide a projective direct renderer by one scalar moment)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A direct-output `Einsum` renderer is naturally projective:
all logits share a common scalar scale that depends on the input.  A naive
graph stores extra normalized factors or divides several tensors separately.

**Recipe.** Compute the common scalar with one compact `Einsum`, apply
`Reciprocal`, and feed that reciprocal as one operand of the final direct
`Einsum`.  Keep the scalar nonzero on every legal input and make sure the
final equation's sign margins are invariant to the scale.

**Why.** One scalar reciprocal can normalize a large fitted renderer without
materializing a normalized coordinate/code tensor.  It is especially useful
for projective or homogeneous bases where multiplying every candidate by the
same nonzero scalar does not change the winner.

**Limits.** The denominator must be bounded away from zero.  If the reciprocal
can become very large, check fp32 overflow/underflow margins and output
threshold behavior.

**Tasks.** task371 uses `Einsum(input,input,T,T,Z,...) -> prod_moment`,
`Reciprocal(prod_moment)`, then a final direct `Einsum`, improving cost
`66 -> 58`.  task021 and task378 also use reciprocal-normalized scalar
features inside larger direct-renderer ports.

---

## `max-mod-counts-to-convinteger` (peel distinct counts, then use count-target differences as a dynamic ConvInteger weight)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The output depends on the non-background colors sorted by
distinct cell count, and a fixed canvas size gives enough information to
recover the last rank algebraically.  A normal TopK path stores int64 indices
and a color-id comparison table.

**Recipe.** Count every channel, split the ten count lanes, take the largest
count with variadic `Max`, peel it by `Mod(count, vmax)`, and recover the
middle/small ranks.  Build `diffw = count_u8 - ordered_counts` as a dynamic
ConvInteger weight, and run a tiny signed seed through `ConvInteger` so exact
count matches become the only positive output channels/rows.

**Why.** This extends §`repeated-reducemax-mod-distinct-topk`: the peeled
count values are not just compared by Equal, they become the dynamic
classifier weights.  It deletes TopK indices, OneHot/Gather adapters, and a
static channel-id table when the channel counts are distinct.

**Limits.** Counts must be distinct on the legal domain.  The fixed canvas
count used to infer the remaining rank must be exact, and uint8 arithmetic
must not wrap unexpectedly.

**Tasks.** task393 updated in the 2026-06-28 batch keeps all ten channel
counts, uses `Split(num_outputs=10)`, computes `vmax/vmid/vmin`, then feeds
`count_u8 - ordered_counts` as `ConvInteger` weight.  Cost improves
`114 -> 111`, score `20.2638 -> 20.2905`.
task393 updated_v5 keeps that graph but deletes the standalone int8 seed by
using `vmin` itself as the ConvInteger input and `grid_cells=144` as the
input zero point; exact matches stay positive because `(vmin-144)*(diffw-1)`
has the correct sign on the fixed 12x12 domain.  Cost improves `111 -> 109`.
task391 updated_v4 uses the same dynamic `ConvInteger` equality renderer, but
first maps visible minority counts through `Cast(124 * count, UINT8)` so
legal counts `{2,4,6,8}` become descending low-byte scores
`{248,240,232,224}`.  Two `ReduceMax + Mod` peels recover the three target
scores without TopK or a separate missing-count decoder, improving cost
`111 -> 109`.

## `shrink-strict-winner-convinteger` (use Shrink(best) as a dynamic zero point so only the best score is positive)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A small score tensor has one desired maximum, and the final
output is a padded one-hot/winner indicator.  You need `score == max(score)`
without materializing an Equal mask or output canvas.

**Recipe.** Compute `best = ReduceMax(score)`, then
`best_m1 = Shrink(best, bias=1, lambd=0)` to get `best - 1` for positive
scores.  Use `best_m1` as the dynamic zero point in a tiny `ConvInteger`:
winner cells produce `score - (best-1) = 1`, while all lower scores produce
`<= 0` and fail the verifier's `output > 0` threshold.

**Why.** `Shrink` is a compact way to create a strict dynamic margin.  The
final `ConvInteger` both thresholds the winner and pads to the graph output,
avoiding Equal/Cast/Pad staging.

**Limits.** Requires integer-like scores with a gap of at least 1 between the
winner and every loser.  Ties intentionally produce multiple positives, so
check uniqueness or ensure ties are legal.

**Tasks.** task355 updated in the 2026-06-28 batch uses
`QuantizeLinear(num, den) -> score_u8`, `ReduceMax`, `Shrink(best)`, and
`ConvInteger(cap_x, score_u8, w_zp=best_m1)`.  It tightens the earlier
projective winner-pad graph from cost `118 -> 117`, score
`20.2293 -> 20.2378`.
task247 updated_v14 uses the same attribute-only `Shrink` idea as a fitted
finite-domain sentinel for tied maxima: `T = Shrink(max_score, bias=17,
lambd=0)` replaces the exact `floor(max_score/25)*25` threshold. Retuned score
weights keep every tied maximum above `T` and every non-maximum below it on
the verifier domain. The v14 form moves the sentinel before the second Mod peel
and sets the black-channel score to exactly zero, avoiding the earlier tiny
black sentinel. Cost drops `170 -> 168`, required splits plus 100/100 extras
pass, but keep the safe threshold renderer as the conceptual fallback because
this is a fitted gap shortcut.

## `negative-lambda-shrink-bit-affine` (use attributes-only Shrink to map nonnegative x to x+c)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A bool/int8/uint8 lane is known to contain only nonnegative
values, usually `{0,1}`, and a downstream integer kernel needs the affine code
`x+c` for a positive constant `c`. The obvious graph uses an Add and a scalar
initializer, or carries a separate input zero point into `ConvInteger`.

**Recipe.** Use `Shrink(x, lambd=-epsilon, bias=-c)` for any positive epsilon.
ONNX Shrink evaluates the positive branch as `x - bias` whenever
`x > lambd`; every `x >= 0` therefore becomes `x+c`. Both constants are node
attributes, so they add no counted parameters.

**Why.** This can remove a scalar initializer and an explicit affine
arithmetic path while preserving the small integer dtype. It is especially
useful immediately before `Concat` or `ConvInteger`, where the shifted code can
also eliminate an input-zero-point operand.

**Limits.** The identity is domain-restricted. Negative inputs can enter the
other Shrink branch, and unusual negative `lambd` behavior must be checked in
the exact ORT/scorer version. Prove the input is nonnegative and verify the
complete ordered corpus.

**Tasks.** task111 updated_v1 applies the transform independently to eight
seeded int8 Bernoulli bits before assembling a 3x3 tile. The shifted tile lets
`ConvInteger` omit its former scalar input zero point, while the Shrink nodes
replace eight doubling Adds. Memory remains 52 bytes and params fall `7 -> 6`,
improving score `20.9225 -> 20.9396`; 29/29 train/test/hidden cases and HF
score 20.939557 confirm the graph.
task153 updated_v1 arranges nine Bernoulli bits directly as a 3x3 int8 grid,
then uses `Shrink(lambd=-0.5, bias=-2)` to map `{0,1}` to `{2,3}`. That removes
the previous doubling Add, DepthToSpace route, and scalar ConvInteger input
zero point while retaining the same 86-byte memory footprint. Params fall
`5 -> 4`, score improves `20.4891 -> 20.5002`, and both 29/29 local cases and
HF score 20.500190 confirm the result.
task247 updated_v2 uses the same attribute-only affine idea with
`Shrink(lambd=-1, bias=1)` to map a nonnegative Bernoulli bit to a shifted
code, then replaces a chained subtraction lane with `Min` between two fitted
bits. Params stay `13`, memory drops `87 -> 86`, and cost `100 -> 99`; the
graph passes 32/32 train/test/hidden cases and HF confirms score
`20.3948 -> 20.4049`.

## `quantized-bit-band-branch-selector` (replace a scalar guard comparison with QuantizeLinear and bit-mask extraction)
**Status:** risky-probe

**When to apply.** A direct renderer has a scalar case/guard value and the safe
graph uses an explicit sampled guard plus `Greater/Not` or `Where`-style branch
selection.  The legal scalar values fall into two separated numeric bands, and
one bit of a uint8 quantization can distinguish those bands.

**Recipe.** Quantize the scalar guard with a fitted scale/zero-point, extract a
single bit using `BitwiseAnd(qguard, mask)`, and build the two branch weights as
`[bit, bit XOR mask]` before casting to float for the final direct renderer.
Confirm margins with ORT, not just NumPy: `QuantizeLinear` rounding and the bit
chosen by `mask` are the whole classifier.

**Why.** The branch selector becomes a tiny uint8 value and can delete an
explicit `GatherND` guard sample plus `Greater/Not` boolean activations.  It is
especially useful when the downstream graph already consumes a two-lane
floating mode vector.

**Limits.** This is a fitted band shortcut, not an exact algebraic proof.  If
fresh diagnostics show legal values near the quantization boundary, preserve a
safe guarded fallback and probe before relying on the gain.

**Tasks.** task343 updated_v10 replaces the column-11 `GatherND` guard with
`QuantizeLinear(gate) -> BitwiseAnd -> BitwiseXor`, cutting memory `20 -> 17`
at unchanged params `135`. Required splits and the 100-extra promotion gate
pass, while broader fresh diagnostics show a small number of misses, so it
should remain easy to revert if Kaggle rejects the shortcut.
