## `sliding-band-path-direct-einsum` (render a long path or replay chain with repeated banded selector matrices in one output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task follows a long 1-D/2-D path, replay chain, or local
transition corridor, and the exact graph currently materializes each step as a
scan/flood/pool/copy tensor.  The transition at each step is local and can be
represented by a fixed banded row/column selector such as a width-2 or width-3
matrix.

**Recipe.** Store only the banded transition matrices and small channel factors,
then feed the original input repeatedly into one graph-output `Einsum`.  Each
input occurrence represents one path step or witness position; each transition
matrix occurrence advances the path.  Because the final `Einsum` is the model
output, all intermediate path canvases disappear from the memory score, and
reusing the same selector initializer many times is counted once.

```python
T[i, j] = 1 if j in {i-1, i, i+1} else 0
output = Einsum(T, input, T, input, ..., channel_factors,
                equation="...->nchw")
```

**Why.** This is the high-gain version of direct-output collapse for tasks that
look inherently sequential.  The scorer charges the selector matrix params but
does not charge repeated references or the graph output.  It can replace a
large materialized replay chain with a single high-arity contraction.

**Limits.** The high-arity equation can be slow or numerically fragile.  Fit or
derive margins on the complete finite generator domain when possible; otherwise
keep it as Kaggle-batch/portfolio-confirmed rather than assuming broad
algorithmic generality.  Watch ORT `Einsum` operand order if local runtime is
large.

**Tasks.** task243 team port is the strongest confirmed example: one repeated
band matrix `T[30,30]` plus five small channel/role factors replaces a large
path/replay graph, dropping cost `6358 -> 1160` and improving score
`16.2425 -> 17.9438` in the 2026-06-29 batch.  task004 uses left/right band
selectors `L/R` and tied rank-5 channel factors in the same style, reducing
cost `2946 -> 2020` and score `17.0118 -> 17.3891`.  Related direct path
ports in the same batch include task089 and task077, though those use larger
spectral/CP factors instead of explicit band matrices.
The 2026-07-01 task004 leaderboard port is the stronger variant of the same
idea: it keeps one graph-output `Einsum` but replaces the broad banded factors
with compact `LOW/HIGH` local transition tensors plus a channel/column gate,
improving the already-confirmed path renderer from cost `1995 -> 818`, score
`17.4016 -> 18.2931`.  A later HF leaderboard `task004` port compresses that
gate again: the old broad `KC_GATE[10,30]` is replaced by a factorized
`GATE_C[30,2]` and one reused colour embedding factor inside the same output
equation.  The factorization deletes 240 params without adding memory, moving
task004 from cost `818 -> 578`, score `18.2931 -> 18.6404`, while passing
required splits and `100/100` promotion extras locally.
The 2026-07-01 HF leaderboard refresh compresses the relation path again:
`LOW/HIGH` become compact `RL/RH` local relation tensors, the broad transition
gate is removed, and one output `Einsum` keeps only `B0/B1/RL/RH` plus small
channel cores.  Cost drops `578 -> 384`, local score `18.6404 -> 19.0494`,
with required splits and `100/100` promotion extras passing.
task004 updated_v3 removes the separate high-digit no-wrap relation entirely:
the low-digit carry split keeps exact wrap information, while high-digit
relation operands reuse the existing cyclic predecessor tensor `RM`.  The only
extra cyclic witness is neutralized by row/colour support and the other gates
on generator-valid samples.  This keeps the one-op memory-zero renderer,
drops params `384 -> 336`, and passes required splits plus `100/100`
promotion extras locally.
task004 updated_v8 keeps the same coordinate renderer but shares the local-rule
core: the old `CD[2,2,2] + BF[2,2] + GA[2,2,2,2]` branch/channel budget is
replaced by `CD[2,2,2] + BG[2,2] + LC[2,2,2]`, where `BG` is used both for
the z-gate branch and black-vs-foreground channel sign.  Params drop
`336 -> 328`, memory remains `0`, and required splits plus `100/100`
promotion extras pass.  task004 updated_v11 compresses the tail further by
replacing the two-lane active/foreground embedding with one signed scalar code:
black maps to a large negative value and all foreground colours map to `+1`.
Four shifted scalar probes plus current-cell/row colour evidence feed a fitted
small core in the final direct-output `Einsum`, dropping params `328 -> 314`
with memory still `0` and required splits plus `100/100` extras passing.
task004 updated_v15 then deletes the remaining explicit branch/identity
factors: one branch is synthesized as `sum_g CR[g,t,b]` from the existing carry
table, and the left-shift identity is expressed by reusing the same `t` label
instead of storing a `2x2` matrix.  This drops params `314 -> 306` while
keeping the one-node memory-zero graph and passing required splits plus
`100/100` extras.  task004 updated_v17 uses inactive coordinate rows as
scratch factors: tail rows of the already-counted `B0/B1` selectors encode a
rank-3 correction whose outer product replaces the explicit local `CD[2,2,2]`
tensor.  Active rows remain the normal coordinate selectors, while tail rows
synthesize the local core inside the output `Einsum`.  This drops params
`306 -> 298`, keeps memory `0`, and passes required splits plus `100/100`
extras.
task089 updated_v2 is a slow local variant using the same one-output
contraction style: four repeated `CM + RP + RP` triples are precontracted into
one `KCM[2,2,2]`, and the 3-cell gate `M3` is synthesized from the already
counted Fourier table with two small vectors.  Cost would drop `616 -> 590`,
but arc-gen[0] smoke estimated `218s` for required splits, so it is preserved
under `src/research/variants/` for later probing rather than promoted.
task089 updated_v3 deletes the remaining two-element `M3V` gate too by using
the diagonal of already-counted `KCM`: repeated labels such as `KCM[f,f,f]`
inside the `Einsum` supply `[1,0]` without an initializer.  This further

## `single-vector-high-order-direct-einsum` (store one coordinate or role vector and synthesize the full renderer from repeated self-products)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A fixed-domain task has a finite spatial/role classifier and
the current graph stores several coordinate tables, small cores, or class
selectors.  If the legal coordinates can be separated by powers/products of one
carefully fitted vector, repeat that vector many times inside a direct-output
`Einsum` instead of storing the tables.

**Recipe.** Search or fit one `Q[30]`/`v[30]` style vector whose low-order and
high-order products distinguish every legal case.  Then use repeated references
to the same initializer in the final equation:

```python
Q = fitted_vector_30
output = Einsum(Q, Q, Q, ..., input, input, equation="...->nchw")
```

For role separation, put tiny, very small, or very large magnitudes in
different coordinate ranges so wrong branches underflow or stay non-positive
under the final `output > 0` rule.  This is often paired with zero rows for
inactive padded coordinates.

**Why.** A repeated initializer is charged once.  Replacing `F[rank,30]` plus
several small cores by a single vector can be a real score improvement even
when the equation becomes visually opaque.

**Limits.** This is usually an offline-fit technique, not an obvious algebraic
identity.  Check fp32/ORT contraction order and sign margins.  If the vector
uses subnormal/underflow separation, keep a safer fallback until Kaggle or a
large extras gate confirms it.

**Tasks.** task028 and task267 both reached `0mem/30param` in the 2026-06-29
batch.  task028 stores one `Q[30]` vector and repeats it more than twenty times
in a single output `Einsum`, improving cost `40 -> 30`.  task267 originally
stored one seven-nonzero role vector `v[30]`, used repeated
input/self-products plus tiny underflow lanes, and also improved `40 -> 30`.
The 2026-07-07 task267 leaderboard graph pushed the same idea further by
splitting a scalar occupancy gate into a separate `Einsum(input,
"bcij->b")`, then using one shared channel vector `G[10]` in the output
contraction.  That replaces the old `F[10,2]` embedding with `G[10]` plus one
4-byte intermediate and improves cost `20 -> 14` (`22.0043 -> 22.3609`).
The same family appears in task236/task347/task078 as `q/E` two-initializer
renderers; task236 drops `70 -> 50` with one coordinate vector and a 10x2
channel embedding.
task143 applies the repeated-factor principle to a small transition core
rather than a coordinate vector. The fitted `M[2,2,2]` relation is replaced
by one `K[2,2]` matrix referenced dozens of times with different contraction
labels, while the seeded Multinomial alphabet is retuned from five symbols to
four. Memory stays 20, params/cost fall `33 -> 28`, and score improves
`21.0297 -> 21.1288`; all 30 known cases pass and HF confirms the exact
graph. When a tiny high-arity core appears repeatedly, search whether powers
and differently labelled copies of a lower-arity matrix span its required
finite-domain behavior.

## `cyclic-color-embedding-direct-einsum` (use a short cyclic color basis inside a direct-output Einsum)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct renderer needs exact equality or
separation among a small fixed palette, but the current graph stores separate
source-color, output-color, and foreground/background equality tables.

**Recipe.** Replace explicit finite color-equality tables with one shared
color basis such as `[1, alpha * is_foreground, cos(2πc/9), sin(2πc/9)]` for
colors `1..9`, plus a tiny metric vector/table inside the final `Einsum`.
Tune the foreground scale and cyclic metric so equal foreground colors stay
strictly positive and all mismatches remain non-positive under the verifier's
`output > 0` rule.  Reuse the same basis for both source and output channel
roles instead of storing separate `C/F0/F1` style tables.

**Why.** The cyclic embedding makes the nine nonblack colors separable with
two phase lanes plus a foreground lane.  Because the basis is referenced
multiple times inside the direct output contraction, ONNX counts it once while
deleting several small explicit equality tables.

**Limits.** This is a margin-sensitive direct-logit trick.  Verify exact
margins on every legal color pair and keep the output as signed logits.  It is
best for fixed-palette generator domains; do not use it for arbitrary learned
colors without a full finite-domain check.

**Tasks.** task005 updated_v1(1) replaces separate `C[10,2]`, `F0[10,3]`,
`F1[10,3]`, and `POA[2,2]` tails with one shared four-lane color/foreground
basis.  The graph remains a single final-output `Einsum` with memory `0`, and
params drop `1194 -> 1162` (`17.9149 -> 17.9421`) with required splits plus
`100/100` extras passing locally.

---

## `rank0-scalar-initializer-factor` (a shape-`[]` one-element initializer can be a safe Einsum factor when it is not an empty-shape Reshape)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A hand-built `Einsum` needs a scalar coefficient many times
and a singleton axis would complicate the equation or require extra labels.
Use a rank-0 initializer only when it is a true one-element constant and it is
consumed as numeric data, not as shape metadata.

**Recipe.**

```python
S = np.array(2e-7, dtype=np.float32)  # shape == (), size == 1
Einsum(F, S, F, ..., equation="a,,b,...->...")
```

**Why.** This clarifies a previously over-broad rule.  Empty initializers and
`Reshape(..., shape=[])` scalarization remain unsafe, but a scalar initializer
with `size == 1` is ordinary tensor data and can be accepted by Kaggle.

**Limits.** Do not use this for `Reshape` shapes, `Resize` roi/scales, or any
metadata/control input.  It is a safety/portability note more than a major
score trick, because `[1]` and `[]` both count as one param.  Prefer `[1]` if
the graph works equally well.

**Tasks.** task041 team port uses rank-0 scalar initializer `S` inside a large
direct-output `Einsum` and was confirmed in the 2026-06-29 81-task Kaggle
batch at cost `81`, score `20.6056`.  The 2026-07-01 promoted task165
leaderboard port uses a rank-0 scalar initializer `V` as a numeric coefficient
inside a two-`Einsum` direct renderer, confirming the same safety rule in a
current batch (`98 -> 97` cost, score `20.4150 -> 20.4253`).

## `role-count-spectral-direct-renderer` (decode finite count/role state, then render through spectral-coordinate factors)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A task has a small finite set of global roles determined by
channel counts or other global signatures, and the output geometry is a regular
path, direction, or adjacency relation.  Instead of a dense role table plus
spatial masks, decode the roles exactly and feed them into a spectral or
low-rank coordinate basis inside one final renderer.

**Recipe.** Use `ReduceSum`, `ReduceL1`, or a compact signature op to produce a
small role code.  Compare it against a few legal role values, cast to fp32, and
contract with spectral/coordinate factors:

```python
cnt = ReduceSum(input, axes=[0, 2, 3])
roles = Cast(Equal(role_values, cnt), FLOAT)
output = Einsum(input, roles, roles, T, Q, U, L, U, ...)
```

If the role signature is already packed, a `TfIdfVectorizer` can replace the
`Equal` decoder; see the TfIdf entries.

**Why.** It keeps the finite global state tiny while letting a low-rank basis
carry the geometry.  This is useful for tasks where a pure coordinate
direct-Einsum would need a large dense relation table.

**Limits.** Role collisions are fatal.  Confirm every legal count/signature,
and keep spectral factors within fp32 margins.  If the required role set is a
Kaggle-distribution shortcut rather than a generator invariant, treat the
candidate as probe-worthy.

**Tasks.** task012 team port decodes three role counts with
`ReduceSum -> Equal -> Cast` and renders through an 11-dimensional spectral
basis, reducing cost `710 -> 610` and improving score `18.4347 -> 18.5865`.
task077 uses a larger direction spectral CP renderer (`dirspec_cp4`) and
improves `886 -> 860` in the 2026-06-29 batch; the previous 2026-06-28 batch
already showed this family can replace much higher-memory graphs.  The
2026-06-30 task012 retune replaces the explicit `Equal -> Cast` role one-hot
with polynomial powers of the global count vector and is documented below;
it reduces cost further from `610 -> 514`.
task117's 2026-07-01 leaderboard retune keeps the same pattern with a compact
`HardSigmoid` role gate and four `Einsum`s, trimming the final renderer
factors from cost `311 -> 305`, score `19.2602 -> 19.2797`.

## `pow-count-role-code-direct-renderer` (use polynomial powers of global counts instead of one-hot role decoding)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A finite role/count state is already represented by small
integer global counts, and the final renderer only needs to separate a few
legal count cases.  A one-hot decoder (`Equal`/`Cast` or a lookup) may cost
more memory than passing polynomial count features directly to the renderer.

**Recipe.** Compute the global count vector once, then use `Pow` with small
constant exponents such as `[0, 1, 2]` to produce a tiny polynomial feature
basis.  Feed that basis into the spectral/direct renderer instead of an
explicit role one-hot:

```python
ReduceSum(input, axes=[0, 2, 3]) -> cnt
Pow(cnt, [0, 1, 2]) -> cnt_pow012
Einsum(input, cnt, cnt_pow012, cnt_pow012, spectral_factors, ...) -> output
```

**Why.** For small legal finite count sets, low-degree polynomial features can
separate roles while deleting boolean comparison tensors and role lookup
initializers.  The renderer can absorb the role decoding in its fitted factors.

**Limits.** This is only safe when the legal count tuples are finite and
separable by the chosen powers.  Check every generator-valid count tuple; if a
hidden count aliases another role, the final output will be wrong everywhere
for that case.

**Tasks.** task012's 2026-06-30 team retune changed the role decoder to
`ReduceSum -> Pow(cnt,[0,1,2]) -> direct spectral Einsum`, improving the
already-confirmed role-count renderer from cost `610 -> 514`, score
`18.5865 -> 18.7577`.
task301's 2026-07-01 leaderboard retune is the same idea in miniature:
`ReduceSum(input)` feeds `Pow(counts,[0,1])`, and the count powers are consumed
directly by one output `Einsum`; the promoted graph cuts cost `234 -> 226`,
score `19.5447 -> 19.5795`.
task012's 2026-07-02 follow-up keeps the same one-node renderer but observes
that its learned 3x3x3 relation tensor is symmetric in the two role axes; a
shared rank-4 product `Qs[k,p] * Qv[t,p] * Qv[z,p]` replaces the dense tensor,
cutting cost `477 -> 474`, score `18.8325 -> 18.8388`, with 100/100 extras.

## `conv-input-as-weight-modpoly-tail` (use a one-byte modular polynomial to turn a self-correlation Conv score into dynamic ConvInteger weights)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A static input-as-weight `Conv(input,input)` produces a tiny
integer-like score, and the remaining task is to map a few score cases to
output channels.  A normal 1x1 classifier or table costs more params than one
carefully chosen byte constant and a small polynomial in uint8 arithmetic.

**Recipe.**

```python
sf = Conv(input, input, kernel_shape=[30, 30], pads=[...])
s = Cast(sf, UINT8)
z = np.array([138], dtype=np.uint8)
a = s * z
b = a + z
q = b * b
d = q + q
W = Concat(s, q, d, a, s, s, b, s, s, s, axis=0)
output = ConvInteger(b, W, w_zero_point=z, kernel_shape=[1, 1])
```

Tune `z` and the polynomial lanes so the legal scores produce positive logits
only for the desired channels.  Because uint8 arithmetic is modular, the same
few operations can create several non-linear residues without a lookup table.

**Why.** It extends the static-input `Conv` exception with a tiny dynamic
classifier tail.  The task056 retune stores only one initializer byte; the
rest of the channel weights are runtime values derived from the self-correlation
score.

**Limits.** This is a finite-domain separator.  Check every legal score and
watch uint8 wraparound deliberately; accidental wrap can pass public examples
while failing hidden cases.  Keep the initial `Conv` weight exactly as the
original input tensor with static attributes, per §`conv-input-as-weight-static-shape`.

**Tasks.** task056 2026-06-29 team port improves the earlier confirmed
input-as-Conv version from cost `21 -> 20`, score `21.9555 -> 22.0043`.

## `bitpacked-column-scan-lowbit` (pack rows into uint16/uint32 bitfields and use lowbit peeling for column transition search)
**Status:** current

This is the scan-oriented extension of §`einsum-pow2-column-bitset`.

**When to apply.** The rule needs column run starts, holes, parity, or a small
number of connected intervals, and a direct `MaxPool`/prefix scan would
materialize many full-column states.

**Recipe.** Pack each relevant colour into an integer bitfield using powers of
two, then use bitwise arithmetic to find transitions and peel the first few set
bits:

```python
bits = Cast(Einsum(input, colour, pow2_rows), UINT16 or UINT32)
starts = bits ^ (bits & (bits << 1))
low0 = starts & (0 - starts)
rem = starts ^ low0
low1 = rem & (0 - rem)
```

Use `Div`/`Mod` by the low bits to shift each run into a local frame, or
compare bitfields directly for parity/adjacency predicates.

**Why.** It turns a vertical scan into scalar integer logic.  The activation
memory is the packed per-column tensor plus a few scalar/column intermediates
instead of many `(H,W)` masks.

**Limits.** The active height must fit the integer width and the packing must
be exact under the chosen dtype.  Add absent sentinels before division.  This
is not a substitute for arbitrary unbounded connected-component labeling.

**Tasks.** task157 and task204 were confirmed in the 2026-06-29 team batch.
task157 uses `uint16` row packs, lowbit peeling, and small
`QLinearMatMul`/`Gather` decoders to improve cost `1310 -> 1126`.  task204
uses `uint32` black/blue column bitfields and transition/parity logic to trim
cost `2927 -> 2923`.
The 2026-07-01 task157 leaderboard retune keeps the same row-pack/lowbit
architecture and saves another five params by replacing one equality lane with
a fitted `Less` branch, improving cost `1126 -> 1121` and score
`17.9736 -> 17.9780`.
task216 updated_v35 applies the same lowbit/log2 idea to object rectangles:
pack blue/red occupancy into row and column `uint32` bitfields, compute
top-left candidates with `occ & ~(prev | left_shift)`, decode first/last set
columns by lowbit and `Log/QuantizeLinear`, then select the red-densest
rectangle before a dynamic crop.  It replaces the previous RoiAlign-heavy
window finder, improving cost `3605 -> 3276` and score `16.8099 -> 16.9056`.
task216 updated_v48 rebuilds the same family around packed bitset/object
records plus finite-tail repair and renders directly to graph output with an
`Einsum`; removing the dynamic `Slice`/`Pad` crop from the counted graph drops
cost `3276 -> 1900` while still passing required splits and 99/100 promotion
extras.

## `finite-domain-min-branch-selector-fold` (replace a zero-test and Where branch with `Min(idx, K)` when the generator skips the middle range)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A runtime integer index controls a two-sided branch, and the
legal generator domain is split as `{0}` vs `{K..max}` with no values in
`1..K-1`. Typical shape: `Equal(idx, 0)` feeds two `Where` nodes to choose a
left/right tap for a dynamic convolution or selector table.

**Recipe.** Replace the boolean zero test with a clipped index:

```text
right = Min(idx, K)
left  = K - right
```

For legal inputs, `idx=0` yields `(left=K, right=0)` and every `idx>=K` yields
`(left=0, right=K)`. The missing middle values are generator-forbidden, so the
clip is an exact branch decoder over the official domain.

**Why.** This deletes the `Equal(idx,0)` activation and usually two `Where`
nodes or one small constant cap. It is a small but safe memory/op cut when the
domain gap is proven from the generator or all required samples and a matching
extra diagnostic.

**Tasks.** task382 updated_v19 folds `cyan_idx == 0` into `Min(cyan_idx, 2)`,
cutting cost `1330 -> 1329` with required `266/266` and extras `100/100`.

**Limits.** Do not use when hidden inputs can contain middle values. If
`idx=1..K-1` is possible, this changes branch weights rather than just folding
the implementation.

---

## `direct-einsum-selector-symmetry-tie` (merge symmetric selector tables by reusing a freed small label as a permutation)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** A memory-zero direct `Einsum` renderer carries paired small
selector tables that are the same up to a finite coordinate permutation, and
another nearby selector path uses a small label only to distinguish the same
finite cases. This is common in fitted direct renderers where row/column or
left/right gates differ only by `y -> y xor k`, group parity, or a two-way
orientation flip.

**Recipe.** Prove an exact table symmetry on the generator-valid support, then
merge the paired tables and spend the freed label on a tiny permutation table.
For task364:

```text
DSC[y, u, s] == DSR[y ^ 2, u, s]
CGAR[X, v, s], CGAC[X, v, s] -> one CGY[X, y, s]
remove the old MGRP[y, v] group operand
add PY[y, v] = onehot(y ^ 2)
rewrite DSC(y,u,s) as DSR(v,u,s) after PY(y,v)
```

**Why.** This can delete two medium selector tables and replace them with one
combined table plus a tiny permutation table. It is especially useful when the
renderer already has enough constraints downstream that the merged gate does
not admit new positive logits. Operand order still matters: consume the
permutation and combined selector near the affected factors so ORT does not
materialize a much larger left-fold scratch.

**Tasks.** task364 updated_v4 deletes `DSC`, `CGAR`, and `CGAC`, adds `PY` and
`CGY`, and drops cost `2852 -> 2844` with required `266/266` and extras
`100/100`. task364 updated_v7 continues the same finite-table audit by finding
an exact rank-2 factorization for the remaining signed selector matrix on the
generator-valid support, reducing params `2844 -> 2811` while keeping memory
zero and promotion extras `100/100`.
task364 updated_v10 keeps the v7 rank-2 selector factorization and additionally
merges the signed background/blue state tail into the same direct-output
renderer. Params drop `2811 -> 2797`, memory stays `0`, and required splits
plus `100/100` promotion extras pass.

**Limits.** Only use after checking the actual tensors or solving the finite
state table. A symmetry that holds visually can fail once signed-logit margins,
inactive channels, or generator-forbidden states are included. Re-run an
arc-gen smoke runtime estimate because a table tie can be algebraically smaller
but slower if the new label order makes ORT keep a larger intermediate.

## `packed-sparse-record-stream-renderer` (finite signature selects packed sparse cell records, then ScatterElements renders)
**Status:** current

**When to apply.** The task has a small finite set of generator-valid output
layouts, each output is sparse or crop-bounded, and the input can be reduced to
a compact signature. A dense output LUT or per-cell classifier is too expensive,
but storing only the changed cells is small.

**Recipe.** Hash the input into a small integer residue, use a metadata table
to recover `(width, height, record_start, record_count)`, slice a static
`uint64` record stream, and unpack several records per word:

```text
words = Slice(word_stream, start, start + count)
records = Cast(BitShift(words, [0,16,32,48]), UINT16)
idx = records // BASE
label = records % BASE
flat = ScatterElements(zeros(height * width), idx, label, reduction="max")
output = Equal(Pad(Reshape(flat, [1, height, width])), class_ids)
```

The record table can live in initializers while the bulky expanded canvas is
runtime-produced. Keep the base large enough to encode labels and indices
without collisions, and keep value_info shapes conservative so static shape
inference and runtime memory accounting agree.

**Why.** This moves cost from full-grid memory/classes into a short packed
stream and a fixed scatter tail. It is often cheaper than a dense
`Gather`/`Equal` case LUT when each case only has a small number of non-default
cells.

**Tasks.** The 2026-07-10 HF-confirmed task018 port uses an `Einsum` key,
42-entry metadata table, packed `uint64` word stream, `BitShift` unpack, and
`ScatterElements(max)` to render a 24x24 sparse label grid before padding to
30x30. It improves local cost `3539 -> 3425` and score `16.8284 -> 16.8611`.

**Limits.** This is a finite-domain technique. Prove the signature has no
collisions on the intended gate, and avoid using it as a memorized training
lookup. If the metadata can choose a zero-length slice, test the scorer path:
some ONNX Runtime builds reject shape-zero reshape patterns even when static
shape inference accepts the graph.
